The next spring, the first class of eight kids came. Grandpa Walt showed up every Saturday to watch. He told everyone who would listen that he had spent twenty years collecting the boards for a building he never could have imagined.

succ3-new-builder-new-work.title: What Arthur Prepared
succ3-new-builder-new-work.body: Arthur ran a small print shop for thirty-five years, printing church bulletins, wedding invitations, and business cards for the whole town. In his last years he could see that the world was changing and that his kind of print shop would not last. He also saw what his son, David, could do: design work, websites, signs, things Arthur barely understood. Arthur knew he could not build that new business himself. So he spent his final five years doing something no one quite understood at the time. He paid off every debt the shop owed. He saved steadily, putting money aside every month in an account with David's name on it. He trained his two best employees in new skills and kept them on through hard years so they would be there for his son. He paid off the building. He visited the town's business owners one by one and introduced David to each of them. When people asked what he was doing, he said only that he was getting things ready. Arthur died at seventy-four, a year before David was ready to take over. At the reading of the will, David discovered the account, the paid-off building, the trained staff, and a letter that said: I could not build what you will build. But I could gather what you need. The Lord chose you for this work, not me. Take courage and build it. David built a design and sign company in his father's old shop. It thrived. Every time he unlocked the front door, he remembered that his father had spent his final years preparing for a work he would never see.

succ4-cross-what-we-could-not.title: Across the River
succ4-cross-what-we-could-not.body: Grandma Rose had run the family quilt shop in the old river town for forty-two years, but the town was shrinking, and the shop's future was on the other side of the river, in the growing city where young families were moving. Everyone agreed the shop needed to move. Grandma Rose also knew that at eighty, she could not lead it there. It would take years of new customers, a new building, and new ways of selling. So one Saturday morning before opening, she gathered the whole staff and her grandson Ethan, who was twenty-eight and had worked in the shop since he was a boy. She stood at the front counter and said, in front of everyone, "I brought this shop as far as I could. I can't take it across the river. Ethan will." Then she turned to him and took both his hands. "Take heart. It's a big river, but you won't cross it alone. The Lord who kept this shop for forty-two years is already on the other side waiting for you." Ethan's eyes filled with tears. The staff clapped. Some of the older women cried. The move took two years and was harder than anyone expected. But every time Ethan doubted himself, he remembered that morning at the counter, and that his courage was not supposed to come from being like his grandmother. It came from the One who went before them both. On opening day in the new shop, Grandma Rose came across the river to cut the ribbon, and she told everyone it was the best day of her life.

succ4-cross-what-we-could-not.title: The Commissioning at the Hospital
succ4-cross-what-we-could-not.body: Samuel had spent twenty years building his family's small medical-supply company, and he had brought it to the edge of the biggest step in its history: a contract that would double its size and require a new warehouse in another state. Then, at fifty-eight, he was diagnosed with a cancer that would not be beaten. He would not live to see the expansion. From his hospital bed, he called his daughter, Miriam, who was thirty-two and had worked beside him for ten years. He also asked the company's twenty employees to come, a few at a time, over two days. When they had all come, he asked Miriam to stand by his bed, and he said to each group what he wanted them all to hear: that he had brought the company as far as he could, that Miriam would lead them across into what he could not, and that they should follow her. When the last group had gone, he held her hand. "Don't try to be me," he said. "You can't be, and you don't need to be. Your courage doesn't come from copying me. It comes from the Lord. He is already ahead of you, and He has never once let this family down." Samuel died two weeks later. The expansion was hard. Miriam made decisions her father would never have made, because she faced problems he never faced. But at every hard moment, she remembered what he had said in that hospital room. The company crossed into its new season under her leadership, and it is still serving hospitals today, led by the daughter her father commissioned in his final days.

succ5-double-portion-hand-it-forward.title: Twice as Many Apprentices
succ5-double-portion-hand-it-forward.body: Old Mr. Haugen had built cabinets by hand for fifty years, and when nineteen-year-old Clara became his apprentice, he asked her on her first day what she wanted to learn. Most of his apprentices had answered politely: whatever you want to teach me, sir. Clara said, "Everything you know. And then I want to go further." Mr. Haugen raised an eyebrow, and then he laughed. "Good. I'd rather teach someone who wants more than I have than someone who wants less." For six years she learned everything he could teach her: joinery, finishing, how to read wood grain, how to price a job honestly, how to deal with a difficult customer. Then she began to go beyond him. She learned new techniques he had never tried and took on work he never could have done. When Mr. Haugen retired, she took over the shop. But Clara did not stop there. Remembering how he had poured himself into her, she started taking apprentices of her own, two at a time instead of one, and she told each of them the same thing on the first day: you're not only learning this for yourself. You're learning it so you can teach someone else. Years later, at Mr. Haugen's ninetieth birthday party, Clara brought him a framed photograph. In it stood fourteen cabinetmakers, every one trained either by her or by someone she had trained. The old man studied it for a long time. "I taught one," he finally said, his voice rough. "Look what you did with it." Clara smiled. "You taught me to ask for more. And then to give it away."

succ5-double-portion-hand-it-forward.title: The Chain Almost Broken
succ5-double-portion-hand-it-forward.body: Thomas inherited his family's construction company from his father, who had inherited it from his own father. Three generations of builders, and Thomas was proud of every brick. He also kept it all to himself. For twenty years, he made every decision, held every client relationship, and trained no one to replace him. He told himself he was protecting the company. In truth, he was afraid that if he taught anyone everything he knew, he would no longer be needed. Then he had a heart attack at fifty-four. He survived, but for six weeks he could not work, and in those weeks the company nearly collapsed. No one knew the clients. No one knew how to bid the jobs. No one knew where anything was. Lying in the hospital, Thomas thought about his grandfather, who had spent his last years teaching his son everything, and his father, who had done the same for him. He realized he had received the whole inheritance and was about to let it die with him. A friend from church visited and read him a passage from Paul's second letter to Timothy, about handing what you have received to trustworthy people, so that it keeps going after you. Thomas counted the links: his grandfather, his father, himself, and then no one. He wept. When he recovered, he did what he had never done. He chose three young foremen and spent the next five years teaching them everything. He made them teach others. Today the company is run by one of those foremen. And she is training the fifth generation.

bc1-the-whole-chain.title: Ready, Ready, Ready
bc1-the-whole-chain.body: Every link on the little media team at Grace Street was proud of its own work. Tobias framed the pulpit like a painting. Lena kept the slides crisp. Marcus guarded the sound. And every Sunday each of them assumed the stream was somebody else's worry. Then came the Sunday when everything looked perfect in the room and nothing at all reached home. The capture cable behind the camera rack had wiggled half loose, so the computer never received the picture, and the encoder sat waiting for a signal that never came. Tobias had the finest shot of his life, and it went nowhere. On Monday the team sat around a folding table and drew the whole path on a napkin: camera, capture, switching, encoder, stream, screens. Lena tapped each box with her pen. "Every one of these hands its work to the next one," she said. "If one of us drops it, the rest of us are just practicing." So they built a new habit. Before the doors opened, they gathered, and Marcus prayed for the service and for the people watching from home. Then, starting at the camera and walking down the line, each person checked their own link and called out "ready" so the next could hear it. Camera ready. Capture ready. Scenes ready. Encoder ready. Stream live. It took four minutes. The next Sunday a woman across town texted the church office halfway through the sermon to say the picture was so clear she felt like she was sitting in the third row. Tobias read the message out loud, and nobody claimed the credit, because every one of them knew it had taken all of them.

bc1-the-whole-chain.title: The Empty Screen in Room Twelve
bc1-the-whole-chain.body: Mother Hattie had not been inside the sanctuary in three years. Her legs would no longer carry her down the long aisle, so every Sunday at ten forty-five an aide at the care home wheeled her to the television in room twelve, and she waited for the church to appear. One Sunday it did not. The camera rolled, the choir sang, the pastor preached his whole message, and room twelve showed only a gray box and a spinning circle. Devon, the young man who ran the encoder, found the problem afterward. The stream key had been changed during the week, and no one had confirmed the stream was live before the service began. He had watched his own screen, and his screen looked fine. That afternoon Devon drove to the care home. He sat beside Mother Hattie and told her the truth: that it was his link that broke, and that she had been left alone with an empty screen because he had only watched his own small part. She held his hand a long time. Then she told him she had prayed for that broadcast every week since it began, and that she would keep praying for him. Devon went back and changed how the team worked. Now no one says "mine is fine" until the person at the very end of the chain confirms that home can see. Every Sunday someone on the team checks the stream from a phone, the way Mother Hattie would see it. And every Sunday, before anything else, they pray for room twelve by name, because the weakest link sets the strength of the whole, and someone is always waiting at the end of it.

bc2-camera-and-image.title: You Can't Sharpen Soft
bc2-camera-and-image.body: Amos had been running the main camera for two months when he decided the last few minutes before service were for coffee, not for checking. The focus was close enough, he figured, and the switching computer could clean things up later. That Sunday the pastor glanced down at his own monitor during the opening prayer and frowned, because the face looking back at him was a gentle blur, and he realized the whole room, the big screens, and every viewer at home were seeing exactly the same thing. After service Amos found Miss Corinne at the switching desk, sliding every filter she had back and forth. "Can't you just sharpen it?" he asked. She shook her head kindly. "Baby, I can make soft look brighter, and I can make it look darker. I can't make it look like it was ever in focus. The picture is born at your lens. Everything after you only carries what you gave it." Amos took that home and chewed on it. The next week he came in early. He zoomed all the way in on the pulpit microphone, set his focus there, pulled back out, and checked the exposure on a volunteer standing where the pastor would stand. He pressed the locking cable connector until it clicked. When the service began, the image on every screen was clean and steady and clear. The pastor looked down at his monitor during the prayer again, and this time he gave the smallest nod toward the back of the room. Amos did not need anyone to explain it. He had given the whole room one good eye to see through, and that was the job.

bc2-camera-and-image.title: The Only Recording
bc2-camera-and-image.body: When old Deacon Harlan went home to be with Jesus, the church filled to the walls for his homegoing service, and Ezra was given the main camera. He was nineteen and nervous, and the family had asked for one thing: a recording they could keep, because Harlan's brother would speak and his brother's health was failing too. Ezra arrived two hours early. He did not rush. He set his focus on the exact spot at the lectern, then asked the funeral director to stand there so he could check the light on a real face. He watched the exposure until the white of a shirt held its detail and the skin looked warm and true. He made sure the cable to the capture card was locked and seated, because he knew that if the picture was soft or blown out at his camera, nothing downstream could ever give it back. During the service he kept his eyes on his work. He did not chase every movement or wander the frame. When the brother rose, slow and shaking, to speak about the man he had grown up beside, Ezra held the shot still and let it simply be seen. A year later the brother had passed as well, and the widow called the church. She said she watched that recording on the evenings she missed them both, and that she could see every line in her brother-in-law's face, every tear, as clearly as if she were in the front pew again. Ezra never told anyone how hard he had worked that morning. He had kept his eyes on what mattered, and it had been enough.

bc3-light.title: Half a Pastor
bc3-light.body: Isaac loved drama, so when he took over the lighting board he decided the Sunday message deserved a little mood. He dimmed the left side of the pulpit almost to nothing and let a single warm light fall across from the right. In the room it looked striking. On the stream it looked like the pastor had been cut in half. By the second point of the sermon, the church's message line was full. One viewer asked whether the pastor was all right. Another asked, gently, if he was hiding something. A grandmother simply wrote that she could only see one of his eyes and missed the other one. Isaac read them all after service with his face burning. Rosa, who ran the main camera, sat down next to him. "The camera doesn't see the room the way you do," she said. "It only records the light you give it. When you took that side away, my picture lost it too, and there was nothing I could do but watch." So the two of them made a deal. They would talk on the headset before every change. Isaac would bring the light up even and clean across the whole pulpit first, and only then add warmth. Rosa would tell him the moment a face went dark or turned to bright featureless white in her viewfinder. The next Sunday the light was plain and warm and steady, and the pastor looked like himself on every screen. No one sent a single message about the lighting. Isaac checked twice, a little disappointed. Rosa laughed and told him that silence was the compliment. Good light, she said, is the kind nobody notices, because everybody can finally see.

bc3-light.title: Light on the Water
bc3-light.body: The baptismal pool at Mount Olive sat in a deep alcove behind the choir, and on every broadcast for years it had shown up as a murky cave with shapes moving inside it. Families watching from far away saw a splash and a cheer and very little else. Coreyon had noticed that for a long time. So when he learned that Abby, a girl of eleven, was to be baptized on the second Sunday of June, and that her father was deployed overseas and would watch the stream at three in the morning his time, Coreyon spent two evenings in the empty sanctuary. He moved two lights to reach into the alcove. He softened them so the water would not throw hard glare into the lens. He checked the color so her skin would look warm and real instead of gray. He asked Lydia, on camera, to tell him exactly what her viewfinder showed while he adjusted, because a change at his board showed up instantly in her picture. On Sunday the pastor lowered Abby into the water and lifted her up again, and the camera caught every bit of it: her eyes squeezed shut, the drops on her face, the sudden wide smile when she came up. Thousands of miles away, in a dim room, her father watched his daughter rise, and he could see her clearly. He wrote to the church that afternoon. He said he had worried he would only see a shadow, and instead he had seen his little girl's face in the light. Coreyon kept that letter in his toolbox. He had not preached anything. He had simply given the light a place to fall, so a father could see what Yahweh had done.

bc4-obs-switching.title: The Boy Who Loved the Buttons
bc4-obs-switching.body: Jalen was fifteen, quick with his hands, and in love with the switching desk. On his first solo Sunday he cut to a new camera every three seconds. Wide shot, close shot, the drummer, the keyboard, a hand on a guitar neck, back to wide. During the sermon he cut so often that a man watching at home said it felt like riding in the back of a car on a gravel road. Brother Felix, who had directed for twenty years, did not scold him. After service he pulled up a chair and replayed ten minutes of the stream without sound. "Watch it as somebody who came to hear the Word," he said. Jalen watched. Within a minute he wanted to look away. "Good switching is invisible," Felix said. "The people should feel carried, not jostled. You cut on a breath, when the pastor pauses, when the song turns. And you stay ahead of him. When you see him reach for his Bible, the Scripture slide should already be waiting, so you can take it the moment he begins to read." They spent the week building Jalen's scenes properly: the wide shot, the pulpit shot, the Scripture slide with the reading laid out clean, the name graphic for the guest speaker. The next Sunday Jalen sat with his hands in his lap more than on the buttons. He cut slowly and on purpose, on the natural beats. When the pastor opened his Bible, the verse was on screen before the first word left his mouth. Afterward the same man from home wrote in again. He said he had not noticed the camera work at all. Jalen grinned, because now he understood that was the highest praise a director could get.

bc4-obs-switching.title: Holding the Wide Shot
bc4-obs-switching.body: Near the end of a long evening service, the pastor stopped preaching and simply stood still. The music had faded to a single sustained chord on the organ, and he invited anyone carrying a burden to come forward and pray. For a while no one moved. Then one man rose from the back, and then a mother with two children, and then many more, quietly filling the front of the sanctuary. In the booth, Naomi's hand hovered over the switching desk. Every instinct of a young director told her to make it exciting: push in on a weeping face, cut to the crowd, cut to the pastor, cut back. She could feel how dramatic it would look. She also felt how wrong it would be. Those were people praying, not footage. So she did the hardest thing a director can do. She held the wide shot. She let the scene breathe. She made one slow, gentle transition to a camera that showed the front of the room from a respectful distance, where no single face was singled out, and then she left her hands still for nearly six minutes. Days later a note came to the church from a woman in another town who had watched alone in her kitchen. She wrote that the broadcast had been so calm and unhurried that she forgot she was watching a screen, and that she had knelt by her own chair and prayed with them. Naomi did not frame the note or show it around. She simply knew that order on the screen had made room for something holy, and that a calm, steady hand on the switch can be a ministry all by itself.

bc5-cpu-gpu-cuda.title: One Chef and a Hundred Cooks
bc5-cpu-gpu-cuda.body: The youth tech night at Bethel always began with a question nobody wanted to admit they had. This time it was Caleb's. "Why do we call the left and right machines the CPUs if Sister Odette keeps saying they're not?" Sister Odette smiled and set two bowls on the table. Into one she put a single potato and a fine knife. Into the other she poured a mountain of onions and handed out paring knives to the whole room. "The CPU is the master chef," she said, holding up the fine knife. "A few very smart workers. They can do almost anything, but mostly one hard thing at a time. The graphics card is all of you with the onions. Thousands of simple workers doing the same small job at the same moment. When a picture has millions of pixels to work out sixty times a second, you don't want one chef. You want the whole kitchen chopping." Then she showed them last Sunday's numbers. The processor had been running near its limit, stuttering the stream, while the graphics card sat almost idle. Someone had set the switching software to squeeze the video on the processor. "There's a little chip on the graphics card whose only job is encoding video," she said. "Use it, and the chef gets to breathe." Caleb flipped the setting himself. The next Sunday the stream ran smooth from the first song to the benediction, and the processor hummed along with room to spare. Caleb went home and explained it to his little sister with two bowls from the kitchen, which Sister Odette later said was the real proof he had learned it.

bc5-cpu-gpu-cuda.title: The Machinist's Hands
bc5-cpu-gpu-cuda.body: Mr. Wendell Booker ran a lathe for thirty-eight years. When he retired and joined the broadcast team, he felt foolish among the young people who spoke so quickly about cores and encoders. For weeks he only carried cables and kept quiet. But a machinist never trusts a machine he does not understand, so in the evenings he studied. He learned that the processor was a few strong workers doing one hard task at a time, and that the graphics card held thousands of small workers doing the same math together. He learned the difference between the system that puts work onto those many cores and the separate chip that does nothing but encode video. He wrote it all in a spiral notebook in careful block letters. On the night before a large community Christmas program, the stream began dropping frames in rehearsal. The young operators started restarting things at random. Mr. Booker opened the machine's activity view and studied it the way he once studied a part spinning on his lathe. The processor was pinned at the top. The graphics card was barely working. The encoder had been switched back to the processor after an update. He changed it, quietly, and the stream ran clean. The next morning he asked the team leader if he could teach the setting to the newer volunteers, and he did, slowly, with his notebook open. He told them that the same hands that shaped steel for his family were now shaping light for the house of worship, and that knowing your tools deeply is not showing off. It is honoring the work Yahweh put into your hands, and it is the beginning of being able to teach someone else.

bc6-bandwidth-network.title: The Garden Hose
bc6-bandwidth-network.body: Uncle Ray was certain the stream problems were the camera's fault. The picture froze, then lurched, then froze again, so he bought a new camera cable, and when that did not help he ran the whole stream over the building's wireless from a laptop, which made it worse. Priscilla, who ran the media closet, finally invited him to the parking lot with a garden hose and a drinking straw. "Raw video from that camera is a fire hose," she said, turning the water on full. "Billions of bits every second. Our internet upload is this straw. You can't push the fire hose through the straw, so the encoder squeezes the picture down small enough to fit. If we ask for more than the straw can carry, the stream chokes." Then she counted the pipes on her fingers. The fast drive inside the computer is a storage barn, where recordings live, not a network at all. The network cable connects machines to each other and to the internet. The broadcast cable carries the live camera picture. "Every one of those is a different pipe," she said. "When one is too small for what flows through it, you get stutter." Back inside, they measured the real upload speed instead of guessing. It was smaller than anyone had assumed. They set the stream to a size that fit comfortably with room left over, and they ran a proper cable from the streaming computer to the network instead of trusting the wireless. On Sunday the stream held from start to finish. Uncle Ray kept the drinking straw in his shirt pocket for a month and pulled it out for anyone who would listen.

bc6-bandwidth-network.title: Two Days Early
bc6-bandwidth-network.body: The call came on a Tuesday. A young mother in the church had died suddenly, and her family was scattered across four states. The service would be Saturday morning, and dozens of relatives who could not travel were counting on the stream. Priscilla knew the building's connection well enough to know she did not know it well enough. So on Thursday evening she stayed late and counted the cost before she trusted anything to it. She measured the actual upload speed at the hour the service would happen. She checked whether the church's office computers would be syncing files at the same time and asked the administrator to pause them for Saturday morning. She replaced a frayed network cable that had been coiled behind the rack for years. She set the stream's size well under the measured limit, because a stream that fits with room to spare survives a bad minute, and one sized to the edge does not. Then she ran a full private test, an hour long, and watched it from her phone on cellular data, the way a cousin in another state would see it. On Saturday the sanctuary was full, and the stream held steady from the first hymn to the final prayer. Afterward a message came from a grandmother in a care facility who had watched every minute. She said it was the only way she could have been there for her granddaughter's goodbye. Priscilla read it alone in the media closet and sat quietly for a long time. No one in the room had seen the two evenings of work. That was how it was meant to be. The tower builder counts the cost before the day, so that on the day, nobody has to.

bc7-llms-for-broadcast.title: The Helper Who Was Very Sure
bc7-llms-for-broadcast.body: Tamsin was delighted with the new A.I. helper. On Sunday afternoon she gave it the transcript of the morning sermon and asked for a title, a short summary, and three social media captions. In thirty seconds it handed her everything, beautifully worded. She nearly posted it all at once. Then she noticed a line in the summary with a Scripture reference she did not remember the pastor using. She checked the recording. He had never said it. The helper had simply guessed a likely-sounding verse and written it with complete confidence. One caption also gave the guest speaker a last name she was fairly sure was wrong. It was. Tamsin sat back and laughed at herself. The helper was a brilliant guesser of the next word, not a knower. It had never been in the room. So she made herself a rule and taped it to her monitor: the A.I. drafts and finds, a person checks and decides. She went through every reference against the recording and her own Bible, fixed the speaker's name, and kept the parts that were genuinely good, which was most of it. Later that week a member called asking for the message on forgiveness from sometime last spring. Tamsin typed the question into the archive search, which looked for meaning rather than exact words, and the right sermon came up in seconds, saving her an afternoon of scrolling. She checked the date against the service records before sending it. The tool had carried the pastor's words further and faster than she ever could alone, and she had made sure they were still his words when they arrived.

bc7-llms-for-broadcast.title: Brother Silas Reads Along
bc7-llms-for-broadcast.body: Brother Silas lost most of his hearing in his fifties. For years after that he sat in the second pew and caught the sermon in fragments, reading the pastor's lips when he faced forward and losing him whenever he turned. He never complained, but his wife said he went home tired from straining. When the broadcast team set up live captions, the speech-to-text running on a screen near his seat and on the stream, Silas followed an entire sermon from beginning to end for the first time in a decade. He cried quietly through the benediction. The team learned quickly, though, that the captions were near-live and not perfect. One Sunday the pastor read the names of a family who had lost their father that week, and the captions turned one of the names into a common word that made no sense. No one in the room noticed. Silas did. So did the grieving widow, who was watching the stream from home. The next morning Hannah, who managed the recordings, went through the caption file line by line before it was posted with the archived service. She corrected the family's names, every Scripture reference, and every place the machine had stumbled. She called the widow herself to say the record was fixed. After that the team assigned one person each week to watch the captions with a careful eye and clean the archive copy before it went out. Silas thanked them on the church steps one Sunday. He said the machine had given him his church back, and the people had made sure it told him the truth. Hannah thought about that for a long time. The tool carried the Word further. The care was what kept it whole.

bc8-pov-sops.title: What Only Gus Knew
bc8-pov-sops.body: Gus had brought the cameras up every Sunday for eleven years, in an order he could not have explained if you paid him. Main camera first, then the wide, then power to the side screens, then a pause he called letting it settle, then the switching computer, and never the other way around. One winter he caught the flu. The volunteers who filled in did everything, just not in his order, and the switching computer came up before the cameras finished waking. Half the service was spent with a black box where the pulpit should have been. When Gus was well again, the team leader handed him a pair of camera glasses. "Wear these and do it exactly like you always do," she said. "Talk out loud while you work." Gus felt silly at first, narrating to nobody in an empty sanctuary. But he walked his sequence and talked it through, short clips one after another. He kept the glasses pointed at the gear and turned his head away from the pews out of habit, because the rule was clear: the team and the gear, never the congregation. The clips came off the glasses and onto the church's own storage, never anyone else's servers. The church's own A.I. turned his words into a draft checklist, and Gus spent an evening correcting it, adding the reasons he had never written down. Three weeks later Gus was away at his granddaughter's wedding. A sixteen-year-old named Pia read the checklist on a tablet, watched the clips once, and brought everything up in perfect order. Gus watched the stream from the reception hall on his phone and grinned. His secret had finally become everybody's.

bc8-pov-sops.title: The Founding Sequence
bc8-pov-sops.body: Brother Amos Pryor had pointed the first camera at the pulpit thirty years earlier, a borrowed home camera on a wobbly tripod, so the sermons could reach the shut-ins. Everything the broadcast had become grew from that first choice. Now his eyesight was failing, and he was moving across the country to live with his daughter. The team realized with a jolt that most of what made the broadcast work still lived in his head. So in his last month, they asked him to wear the recording glasses and walk them through it all. He did it slowly, over three evenings. How he warmed the room before the cameras came up. Why the main camera went first. What he listened for in the audio before he ever trusted the picture. Which breaker to check when the side screens went dark. Several times he stopped and simply explained why he cared, how he used to picture the faces of the people watching from their beds. He kept the glasses on the equipment and away from the empty pews, as the team had agreed. The clips went straight to the church's own storage, the church's own A.I. drafted his words into checklists, and the team sat with him to correct every line until he said it was right. On his last Sunday he sat in the front pew instead of the booth. A fifteen-year-old named Joel ran the whole founding sequence from the checklist, steady and in order, while Brother Amos listened to it come together around him. Afterward the old man found the boy and held his face in both hands. He did not say much. He did not need to. The work had been written plainly, and it had been handed on.

bc9-excellence-as-worship.title: The Lucky Sunday
bc9-excellence-as-worship.body: Easter at Cornerstone had been flawless. The cameras sang, the light was warm, the stream never hiccupped, and the team went out for pancakes afterward feeling like professionals. The very next Sunday, almost everything went wrong. No one had charged the wireless microphone. The encoder was still set for the special Easter layout. The stream started eight minutes late because nobody remembered the order of confirming it. Over coffee that afternoon, Delphine, who led the team, said what all of them were thinking. "Easter wasn't excellence. Easter was luck. We had the right people standing in the right places, and they all happened to remember everything." So that week they wrote it down. One page, in the order the work flows: power, cameras, light, sound, switching scenes, encoder settings, network, stream confirmed live from a phone. They laminated it and hung it in the booth. The rule was simple. Every Sunday, every item, every time, in order, out loud, even when it felt silly, even on the best day. The first few weeks the list felt slow. By the second month it took six minutes and nobody thought about it. The broadcast was not dramatic anymore. It was simply right, week after week, and the church stopped noticing it, which Delphine said was exactly the point. They were not doing it to impress anyone. The work was for the King, and He was worth a broadcast that worked every Sunday, not only on the ones that happened to go well. When a new volunteer asked what made the team so good, Delphine pointed at the laminated page and said it was the most spiritual thing in the room.

bc9-excellence-as-worship.title: Hands in Her Lap
bc9-excellence-as-worship.body: Mrs. Lorraine Ellis had run the switching desk for fourteen years, and she was very good. That was the trouble. Whenever anything went wrong, people simply waited for her to fix it, and over time the whole broadcast had come to rest on one pair of hands. When her doctor told her she would need to step back for her health, she understood that her greatest work was still ahead of her. She chose a quiet seventeen-year-old named Imani, who had been carrying cables for a year and watching everything. For three months Mrs. Ellis taught her the desk. She explained every scene and why it existed. She taught her to cut on a breath and to stay a step ahead of the service. She had Imani write the checklist in her own handwriting, so it would be hers. Then came the hard part. On a Sunday in the fall, Mrs. Ellis sat beside the desk and folded her hands in her lap. She did not touch a single button. When Imani hesitated during the offering, Mrs. Ellis felt every muscle in her arms wanting to reach over. She kept her hands still and said only, "You know this. Take your time." Imani found the right scene and took it cleanly. Afterward the girl was shaking and laughing at once. Mrs. Ellis hugged her and told her the next assignment was to start teaching the boy who carried cables now. That night Mrs. Ellis wrote in her journal that she had run a thousand services, but that this was the first one she was sure would outlive her. Founders raise founders, and that is how the work keeps serving the King.

inf1-what-is-sovereign.title: The Rented Photo Album
inf1-what-is-sovereign.body: For twelve years the Okafor family kept every photograph on a free service somebody's cousin had recommended. Birthdays, graduations, Grandpa Eli's garden, the twins' first steps, thousands of pictures, all sitting on a company's computers somewhere far away. Then one morning an email arrived. The free plan was ending. To keep their photos, they would need to pay a monthly fee that would rise every year, and until they paid, they could look at the pictures but not download them. Mrs. Okafor read it twice and set her coffee down. "So they're our photos," she said slowly, "but they're in somebody else's house." That weekend her son Daniel came over with a small storage box he had bought, the kind that sits on a shelf and hums. They paid the fee for one month, carefully copied every picture home, and canceled. Then Daniel was honest with them. Owning the box meant owning the chores the company used to do. Somebody had to check that it was healthy, keep a second copy somewhere else, and install the updates. So he wrote it all on one page and taped it inside the closet door, and he taught his younger sister how to do each step so it would never live in only one head. A year later Grandpa Eli asked to see the garden pictures from the summer he planted the peach tree. Daniel pulled them up from the box on the shelf in seconds. Nobody had to pay a ransom for their own memories. They were simply home, kept by people who loved them, tending the little garden of their own family's life.

inf1-what-is-sovereign.title: The Archive That Vanished
inf1-what-is-sovereign.body: Faith Chapel had trusted a hosting company with every sermon its founding pastor ever preached. Nineteen years of messages, all stored on servers the church did not own and could not see. It was convenient. Somebody else handled the machines. Then the company was sold, and the new owners shut down the service with thirty days' notice, sent to an email address no one at the church checked anymore. By the time anyone noticed, the archive was gone. The founding pastor was elderly by then. When the deacons told him, he was quiet for a long while. Then he asked whether anyone had kept copies, and the answer was mostly no. A few dozen messages survived on old discs in a member's basement. The rest were lost. A young member named Terrence took that loss personally. He spent a season learning how to build what the church needed on machines it owned: a storage box in the church office, kept healthy and backed up, with a second sealed copy at a trusted member's home. He was honest with the deacons about the cost. There would be no landlord now to do the chores, so the chores had to be shared and written down. He trained three others to do them. Years later, when another company changed its terms without warning, Faith Chapel did not even notice. Its sermons were sitting in its own building, tended by its own people. Terrence never forgot the pastor's face on the day the archive vanished. He understood now that owning the iron was not about pride. It was stewardship, the simple faithfulness of keeping what had been entrusted, so it could serve the people instead of being held over them.

inf2-the-nas.title: The Barn and the Brain
inf2-the-nas.body: Micah was ten and suspicious of the humming box in the hall closet. It had little green lights, several drawers in the front, and it never turned off. "Is it a computer or a closet?" he asked his dad one evening. His dad laughed and sat down on the floor with him. "Both, sort of. Think of a farm. This half is the barn," he said, tapping the drawers. "Each drawer holds a hard drive, and together they store everything that matters: your baby pictures, Mom's recipes, the recordings of your grandma singing. And this half," he said, tapping the top, "is the brain. It runs little helpers all day long. One sends an alert to my phone if something goes wrong. One makes sure the family's files show up on everybody's devices. One is a small A.I. that helps sort things." Micah frowned. "Then why doesn't it have a cool graphics card like Jordan's gaming computer?" "On purpose," his dad said. "This box is a sturdy barn and a steady brain. It isn't built to be a racehorse. The heavy, fast A.I. work belongs on a different machine." Micah asked how full the barn was. His dad started to guess, then stopped and opened the family app instead, where the storage page showed a real number read from the box that very minute. "We don't remember numbers like that," he said. "We read them from the real thing, so they're always true." Micah nodded seriously and asked if he could be the one to check it every Saturday. His dad said yes, and wrote Micah's name on the closet door chart, right under his own.

inf2-the-nas.title: Grandma Odette's Voice
inf2-the-nas.body: For years Simone's grandmother left voice messages on the family phones. Long, rambling, wonderful ones. A hymn she was humming, a recipe recited from memory, a prayer for a grandchild's exam. Most of the family listened once and let them sit on their phones. But Simone's husband, Andre, had set up a storage box at home and quietly arranged for everyone's phones to save their voice memos and photos to it, every night, across several drives, with a sealed copy kept at the church. He checked it every Saturday and did not think much about it. It felt like stocking a storehouse against a day no one wanted to name. When Grandma Odette went home to be with Jesus, the family gathered in her small apartment, and someone asked whether anyone still had her voice. One by one they checked their phones. A cracked screen here. An old phone replaced and wiped there. Messages lost to the ordinary carelessness of busy lives. Then Andre opened the family app and found the storage box. Four hundred and twelve messages were there, kept safe over six years: the hymns, the recipes, the prayers, each one dated. The room went very still. Simone's mother asked to hear the one from the morning of her own wedding, and Andre found it, and the old woman's voice filled the room, laughing and blessing her daughter. Andre had never thought of the box as holy. But that night he understood what Joseph had understood when he filled the storehouses in the good years. What you gather faithfully in ordinary days is what carries a family through the lean ones.

inf3-storage-raid.title: Two Kinds of Safe
inf3-storage-raid.body: Aunt Bea was very proud of the church's storage box because, as she told everyone, it had four drives and could lose one without missing a beat. So when she cleaned up the shared folders one Tuesday and accidentally deleted the entire choir rehearsal library, three years of recordings, she was not worried at first. "The box keeps copies," she said. "That's what the four drives are for." Her nephew Theo gently explained that the four drives were one kind of safe, not two. The drives protected against a drive dying. When one fails, the box keeps running and rebuilds onto a new one. But when you delete a file, the box obediently deletes it from every drive at once, because that is what you asked it to do. "That's redundancy," he said. "It isn't a backup." Aunt Bea sat down hard. Then Theo smiled, because he had counted the cost a year earlier. He had set up the second kind of safe: a separate copy of everything, sent every night to the church's other building, encrypted and sealed so nobody there could read it. Three copies, on two kinds of media, one of them offsite. And because a backup you have never restored is only a hope, he had practiced restoring a folder once a month. That afternoon he restored the whole choir library from the sealed copy. Every recording came back. The choir director never even knew it had been gone. Aunt Bea baked Theo a pound cake and asked him to teach her the difference properly, so she could explain it to the next person who said four drives meant everything was safe.

inf3-storage-raid.title: The Amber Light
inf3-storage-raid.body: Harold saw the amber light on the storage box at ten o'clock on a Thursday night. One of the drives had failed. Every drive fails eventually, and he had known this day would come, but his heart still sank, because everything the family and the church kept lived in that box. He remembered his cousin's print shop. When a drive failed there, his cousin had rushed, pulled the wrong drive in a hurry, then restarted the box in the middle of rebuilding, and lost seven years of customer work in a single night. So Harold made himself slow down. He made a cup of tea. He opened the box's own status page and confirmed exactly which drive had failed by its number and position, and he wrote it on a sticky note. Then, before touching anything, he checked that the offsite backup had finished its run the night before, and he restored one small folder from it to be sure the copy was real and readable. Only then did he take the replacement drive from the shelf where he kept a spare. He pulled the one failed drive, only that one, checked the number twice, and slid the new one in. The box began to rebuild. It would take most of the night. Harold did not restart it. He did not touch it. He sat nearby with his Bible and his tea and checked the progress every hour, the way a shepherd might sit up with a sick lamb. By morning the light was green again, and nothing had been lost. His wife found him asleep in the chair. Knowing well the state of what you have been given is not fear, he told her later. It is simply love paying attention.

inf4-network-gateway.title: The House With No Inside Walls
inf4-network-gateway.body: When Rosalind first looked at her uncle's network, she said it was like a house with a front door and no inside walls. Everything was in one big open room. The family's laptops, the shared files, the little office computer for the church's books, the smart television in the rental apartment downstairs, the tenant's game console, even the doorbell camera, all on the same network, all able to see one another. "If somebody gets into the tenant's television," she said, "they can walk right over to your family photos." Her uncle frowned. He had never thought of it that way. So Rosalind spent a Saturday building rooms. The gateway, the box where the internet comes into the house, could split one network into several separate ones, each walled off from the others. She made one room for the family, one for the church's office work, one for the rentals, and one for the gadgets like the doorbell and the thermostat. She left the front door guarded, blocking anything from outside that had not been invited in. Then she did the part most people skip. She wrote down every wall on a single page: what each room was for, what could talk to what, and why. "A wall you can't explain is a wall you can't trust," she said, taping it inside the closet. A month later the tenant downstairs mentioned his television had been acting strange, and a repairman found it had picked up something nasty from an old app. Her uncle checked the family room. Nothing had crossed over. He called Rosalind that night just to say the walls had held, and that he finally understood why Nehemiah cared so much about rebuilding them.

inf4-network-gateway.title: The Clinic Down the Hall
inf4-network-gateway.body: The little counseling clinic shared a building with a family business and two apartments. For years they all shared one network too, because it was cheaper and nobody thought about it. The clinic's records held the most private things people ever say out loud: grief, fear, the hardest seasons of their lives. Joanna, the clinic's director, finally asked a volunteer named Mateo to look at how it was protected. He was quiet for a while after his first walk through it. Then he told her plainly that any device in the building could reach the clinic's files. Joanna did not sleep well that night. So Mateo rebuilt it the right way. He set the gateway to guard the front door and to divide the building into separate rooms, so the clinic's network was walled off completely from the apartments and the business. He gave each person one set of credentials matched to their role, so the receptionist could reach the schedule but not the session notes. He set up a way for an outside contractor to get in through a narrow, separate door without ever touching the clinic's room. And he wrote down every wall and every door, so that whoever came after him could understand it. He also set up a watch, alerts that would tell him if anything unusual tried to cross. Eight months later, one of the apartment tenants brought home a laptop that had been infected with something harmful. The alerts caught it trying to reach other machines. It got nowhere near the clinic. Joanna thanked Mateo with tears in her eyes. He only said that walls are good, but walls with a watch are how people stay safe.

inf5-remote-access.title: The Key Under the Mat
inf5-remote-access.body: Cousin Leon wanted to see the family photos from his vacation, so before he left he did what a website told him to do. He opened a door on the home network straight to the internet, so the storage box could be reached from anywhere. It worked. He showed everyone pictures from a beach a thousand miles away. When he got home, his niece Ada pulled up the box's sign-in log and turned the screen toward him. In six days there had been more than nine thousand attempts to log in from strangers all over the world, machines trying password after password. "Uncle Leon," she said, "you didn't just open a door. You put the key under the mat and hung a sign on it." Leon went pale. Ada closed the open door that same evening. Then she set up a private tunnel instead, an encrypted path that only the family's own trusted devices could travel through. From the beach or a hotel, Leon's phone would join the tunnel and reach home, while to the rest of the world, the house simply did not appear at all. A week later the plumber needed to check the smart water heater remotely. Ada did not put him on the family's tunnel. She gave him his own narrow way in that reached only the water heater and nothing else. "Everyone gets exactly the door their job needs," she said, "and no more." Leon asked if that wasn't a little suspicious of the plumber. Ada shook her head. "It isn't suspicion," she said. "It's what keeps everybody safe, the plumber included." The sign-in log stayed quiet after that, which Leon checked every morning for a month, just to be sure.

inf5-remote-access.title: Far From Home
inf5-remote-access.body: Marcus was eleven hundred miles from home when his father was moved into intensive care. In the hospital's family room late that night, the doctor asked whether his father had an advance directive, the document saying what kind of care he wanted. Marcus knew it existed. His father had signed it two years before, and Marcus had scanned it himself and saved it at home, on the family's storage box in the hall closet. He had no paper copy with him, and the house was empty. His hands shook as he opened his laptop. Then he remembered what his sister had set up the winter before. The storage box was not open to the internet, not to strangers, not to anyone who went looking. But his own laptop was one of the family's trusted devices, and it could travel the private, encrypted tunnel that led home. He connected. The folder opened as if he were standing in the hallway. In two minutes he had the document, his father's own signature at the bottom, and he handed it to the doctor. Later, sitting beside his father's bed, Marcus thought about how close he had come to having nothing. If the box had been locked to him, he would have been helpless. If it had been open to the world, the family's most private papers would have been exposed to anyone. Instead the right door had opened for the right person, at the hour he needed it, and stayed shut to everyone else. He thought of the gatekeeper and the shepherd he knows. His father recovered slowly that month, and when Marcus told him the story, the old man said that sounded like being kept.

inf6-local-ai.title: The Patient Little Model
inf6-local-ai.body: Kendrick was fifteen and had just set up a small A.I. model on the family's storage box. He was thrilled that it ran right there in the closet, so nothing anybody typed ever left the house. Then he asked it to write a long summary of an entire sermon series, forty pages of transcripts, and watched it crawl along one slow word at a time. After twenty minutes it had written two paragraphs. Kendrick groaned. His older cousin Naya, who had set up the box, explained. "That box has no graphics card. It's a brilliant storage barn and a steady brain, but it thinks at the speed of its processor. It can run small models, and small models are good at small jobs. The big heavy reasoning waits for a stronger machine." So they gave the little model a job that fit its size. Every night, it would quietly sort the church's incoming feedback notes into a handful of plain categories: building, broadcast, children, music, and other. It did not need to be fast. It had all night. In the morning, Kendrick checked its work, and it had been right about most of the notes and wrong about a few. It had put a complaint about the nursery heater under music, of all places. He laughed and fixed them by hand. "That's the posture," Naya said. "It's a tool. We test it. We keep what's good, and we fix what isn't." By the end of the month the little model was saving the church secretary an hour every Monday, and Kendrick had learned the most important thing about A.I. there is: what it is, what it is not, and to check its work.

inf6-local-ai.title: The Words That Stayed Home
inf6-local-ai.body: Pastor Ellison carried other people's sorrows for a living. Every week people sat across from him and told him things they had never said aloud: a marriage on the edge, a secret debt, a child who had stopped speaking to them. He kept handwritten notes, and over the years they had piled into boxes he could no longer sort. A younger minister suggested he paste them into a free online chatbot to organize them. Pastor Ellison would not even consider it. Those words belonged to people who had trusted him, and he would not send them to a stranger's computer to be stored and read. So the church's tech volunteer, Grace, offered another way. The church had its own small A.I. running on its own storage box, in a locked room in the church office. Nothing typed into it ever left the building. It was not fast, and it was not large, but it could help him group notes by theme and remind him who he had promised to call back. Grace was honest with him about its limits. It could misread his handwriting once it was typed, and it could make a confident mistake. So he checked every summary it produced against his own memory and his own notes, the way he would check any helper. Within a few months he had found three people he had meant to follow up with and had somehow lost track of. He called each of them. One said the call came on the very week she most needed it. Pastor Ellison told Grace afterward that the machine had been useful, but that he had never once mistaken it for wisdom. Wisdom, he said, still comes from Yahweh. The machine just helped him keep his promises.

inf7-gpu-vram-farm.title: The Suitcase and the Closet
inf7-gpu-vram-farm.body: Imani had read about a huge A.I. model online, seventy billion parameters, and she wanted to run it at home on her brother's gaming graphics card. She downloaded it, pressed start, and watched it fail with an error she did not understand. Her uncle Victor, who worked with computers, came over with two things: a giant suitcase and a small hallway closet. "The graphics card is wonderful," he said, setting the suitcase down. "It has thousands of tiny workers who all do the same kind of math at the same moment. That's exactly what A.I. needs. But the model has to fit inside the card's own memory before those workers can touch it. That memory is this closet." He tried to shove the suitcase into the closet. It did not go. "Your brother's card has a small closet," he said. "A model that size needs a closet about four times bigger. It isn't that the card is bad. It's that the suitcase doesn't fit." Imani asked what people did, then. Victor explained that some families and churches build a bigger closet by putting two or three strong cards together in one machine, enough memory for the big models, and that it costs real money, thousands of dollars. "So you count the cost first," he said, "and you're honest about why you're spending it. If all you want is to save a small monthly bill, it isn't worth it. If you want to own your own A.I., with your own data staying home, that's a different reason." Imani chose a smaller model that fit her brother's closet perfectly. It ran fast and well, and she started saving her allowance, which Victor said was the most sensible first step in building anything.

inf7-gpu-vram-farm.title: Not Yet, and Here Is Why
inf7-gpu-vram-farm.body: At the church planning meeting, a member named Gordon stood up full of excitement. He had seen a demonstration of a powerful A.I. and wanted the church to announce, that very month, that it had its own. He wanted it in the bulletin. Deacon Rhoda, who stewarded the church's machines, listened carefully and then told the truth, even though it disappointed him. "Right now we don't have that," she said. "Our storage box has no graphics card at all, by design. The one good graphics card we own belongs to creative work and has to yield to it, so we can't promise it to anyone else. The big machine we've planned, two strong cards with enough memory for the large models, isn't bought yet. It will cost about five thousand dollars." The room was quiet. Gordon asked whether they could at least say they were close. Rhoda shook her head gently. "If we paint a picture that isn't true, people will trust a thing that doesn't exist. I'd rather tell you what we have." Then she named the real resource they did have: the two machines that drive the church's video wall had capable graphics cards, and when the wall sat idle on weekday afternoons, they were the best place to run modest A.I. work for now. She laid out the plan, the cost, and the reason: owning their own A.I. so the congregation's words stayed in their own building, not saving a small monthly fee. The church voted to save toward it over the year. Gordon came up afterward and thanked her. He said he would rather build on a true number than a pretty one. Rhoda said that was exactly what counting the cost meant.

inf8-church-stack.title: Across the Parking Lot
inf8-church-stack.body: Jasmine had spent a year learning her family's home system: the storage box that was both barn and brain, the gateway that walled off the rooms, the private tunnel for reaching it from the road. One Sunday after service, Mother Edna, who had run the church office for twenty-six years, caught her by the elbow. The office computer had frozen again, the volunteer schedule lived on three different paper calendars, and the sermon recordings were on a single drive in a desk drawer. "Baby," Mother Edna said, "I hear you know computers. We can't find anybody who will help a church like ours." Jasmine looked across the parking lot toward her own house and realized the answer was already sitting in her closet. The church did not need something new and strange. It needed the very same pattern, carried across the lot: its own storage box, kept healthy and backed up, with a sealed copy at her family's house and the family's sealed copy at the church, so each protected the other without either one being able to read the other's files. Walls to keep the members' and the money records separate and staff-only. A simple screen for the volunteer schedule. Jasmine was nervous about it. Mother Edna was not. "You start, and you'll learn the rest," she said, waving her hand. "We'll pray you through it." By spring the sermons were safe, the office computer stayed awake, and the schedule lived in one place. Mother Edna still did not love technology, but she loved that it finally worked, and she told every visiting pastor about the young woman who had brought her home system across the parking lot.

inf8-church-stack.title: Unless He Builds It
inf8-church-stack.body: Greater Hope was a large church in a neighborhood the big tech companies did not think about. Its building had been raised by its own members, brick by brick, over a decade of bake sales and offerings. Its office staff were mostly retirees who served for love, not pay. And for years, every time the church asked an outside company for help with its computers, the answer was a price it could not afford or a technician who never came back. Brother Isaiah Dunn had watched that happen long enough. He was not a professional. But he had built a sovereign system for his own household, and he decided to build the same for his church. He began every work night in the empty sanctuary with prayer, asking Yahweh to build the house, because he knew how easy it would be to build something clever that served no one. He set up the church's own storage box and backups. He walled the networks so member and financial records stayed staff-only. He kept the broadcast running and the video wall bright. And he wrote every step down plainly, in language the retired office staff could follow. Then he did something he had not planned. A pastor from a small church across town, facing the very same neglect, asked how Greater Hope had done it. Isaiah handed him the binder. A year later, three other churches in the city were running the same pattern, each tending its own. Isaiah never thought of himself as a builder of anything large. But when he looked at the binder passed from hand to hand, he understood that what Yahweh builds is meant to be given away, and that every evening of the work had been worth it.

inf9-keeping-it-alive.title: The Phone That Buzzed at Breakfast
inf9-keeping-it-alive.body: For years the church's machines had one way of telling anyone something was wrong. Somebody noticed. Usually that somebody was the pastor, on a Sunday morning, when the slides would not load. So when Calvin rebuilt the system, he made it watch itself. Every job had a health check. Every nightly backup reported when it finished. And when anything failed, the system pushed an alert straight to his phone through a little notifier that ran on the church's own storage box. A failure came through marked urgent, so it could not hide among ordinary messages. The first alert came on a Thursday at breakfast. Calvin's phone buzzed hard. The overnight backup had failed because a cable to the backup drive had worked loose. He drove over before work, reseated it, ran the backup by hand, and watched it finish. Total time, twenty minutes. Nobody else ever knew. Under the old way, that broken backup might have gone unnoticed for months. Calvin also liked the health screen in the app. It read real checks from the live machines, and when something was not reporting, it said so plainly, "stale" or "not connected," instead of showing a comforting green light it had not earned. His wife teased him that he loved that screen more than the television. He told her the television had never once told him the truth about anything. On Sunday the slides loaded, the stream started, and the pastor had no idea anything had ever gone wrong. Calvin thought that was the whole point. A good steward does not wait for someone else to discover the problem. He sets a watch, so the problem finds him first.

inf9-keeping-it-alive.title: The Weekend the Machines Ran Away
inf9-keeping-it-alive.body: Before Gloria left for a family reunion, she set the church's automations running. A job that checked the recordings every few minutes. A helper that started new tasks whenever it found something to do. An A.I. that drafted summaries on a timer. Each one seemed harmless by itself. None of them had any limit on how much it could do, any way to know whether the last run had finished, or any way to stop itself if it went wrong. On Saturday night, one job got stuck. The timer kept firing anyway, stacking new runs on top of the stuck one. Each new run spawned more work. The machines in the office roared their fans and filled their memory, and by Sunday morning the whole system had ground to a halt. The slides would not load. The stream would not start. A deacon finally pulled the plugs by hand, one machine at a time. Gloria came home heartbroken. She did not make excuses. She sat with the team and they rebuilt every automation with three brakes. A budget, so any run that reached its limit of time or work would stop itself. A lock, so a new run that found an old one still going would skip instead of piling on. And a switch that would pause the whole thing on overrun or repeated failure, instead of charging ahead. They tested each brake to prove it actually caught the problem. And they agreed that nothing new would run on its own until its brakes had been proven to work. Gloria told the congregation the story plainly the next Sunday. She said keeping a watch day and night was not about distrust. It was how you love the people who depend on a thing to work.

inf10-build-right-raise-builders.title: The Checklist on the Closet Door
inf10-build-right-raise-builders.body: Aunt Pauline built most of the family's system herself, and for three years she was the only one who knew how anything worked. When the storage box needed a restart, everybody called Pauline. When the network went down, everybody called Pauline. When the church's backup needed checking, everybody called Pauline. Then she took a two-week cruise for her fortieth anniversary, and on the third day the internet at the house went out. Her phone did not work at sea. The family sat in the dark for two days, staring at blinking lights, afraid to touch anything. When Pauline came home and heard the story, she was not annoyed. She was ashamed, a little, that she had built something so good and left it so lonely. So she started writing. One page for each part of the system, taped inside the closet door, in plain words. How to restart the box safely. How to tell if the backup ran. What the gateway lights mean. Who to call for what. Then she chose her nephew Darius, who was thirteen and curious, and walked him through each page, letting him do every step with his own hands while she watched. Once he knew a page, he taught it to his little sister. Pauline did the work carefully, not to impress anybody, but because people were depending on it, and because she believed Yahweh saw the work done in a closet as surely as the work done on a stage. The next time the internet went down, Pauline was at choir practice. By the time she got home, Darius had already fixed it, and had written a note on the page about what he learned.

inf10-build-right-raise-builders.title: The Builder Who Fell Ill
inf10-build-right-raise-builders.body: Mr. Cyrus Wade built the church's whole technology stack over seven years, and he built it well. The storage, the backups, the network walls, the broadcast machines, all of it ran smoothly under his hand. But he kept it all in his head. He meant to write it down someday. Then one January he had a stroke. He survived, but for months he could not speak clearly or use his right hand. In that time the church's systems slowly drifted. A backup failed silently. A password expired that only he had known. The church office could not open the giving records for three weeks. Nobody had done anything wrong except trust that Cyrus would always be there. As he recovered, Cyrus understood what had happened, and it grieved him more than his illness had. He had built something faithful and failed to make it last. So when he could speak again, he asked for helpers. Every Tuesday evening two young men from the media team sat with him in his living room. Slowly, with his speech still halting, he taught them each part of the stack. They wrote it down as he spoke. They recorded the procedures in short clips. Then they went to the church and did each step themselves while he watched over a video call. By the end of the year, four people could run everything he had built, and each of them was already teaching someone else. Cyrus told the pastor that his illness had shown him the difference between owning a thing and stewarding it. You only truly own a part of the work, he said, when you can hand it to someone faithful, who can hand it on again.

dsi1-what-poetech-is.title: The Drawer Full of Apps
dsi1-what-poetech-is.body: When Brenda took over as church administrator, her predecessor handed her a sticky note with eleven passwords on it. One for the giving site, one for the choir's song list, one for the calendar, one for the volunteer schedule, one for the sermon videos, and on and on. Every Monday Brenda opened all eleven, copied numbers from one to another, and hoped they agreed. They rarely did. The giving site said one thing, her spreadsheet said another, and the report to the deacons said a third. Then the church moved to one app. The giving, the choir, the order of service, the Scripture library, the lessons, all in one place, on her phone or the office computer, still working when the basement had no signal. Brenda was skeptical until the first deacons' meeting. A deacon pointed at a number on the screen and asked where it came from. Brenda tapped it, and the app showed her: the real records it was built from, each with a date. Another card on the screen simply said "not connected yet," because the old building fund account had not been linked. The deacon frowned at it. "Why not just put an estimate there?" he asked. Brenda surprised herself with the answer. "Because a made-up number on a page about the church's money is worse than no number at all. When it's connected, it'll show the real one." The deacon thought about that and nodded slowly. That night Brenda threw away the sticky note with the eleven passwords. She had one place now, and everything in it was true or honestly said it was waiting.

dsi1-what-poetech-is.title: The Balance That Wasn't There
dsi1-what-poetech-is.body: After her husband passed, Mrs. Loretta Hayes took over the household money for the first time in forty years. Her nephew set her up with a free budgeting program that showed a cheerful balance at the top of the screen. What he did not realize was that the program filled in an estimate whenever it could not reach the bank, and it never said so. For three months it reached the bank only now and then. Mrs. Hayes trusted the number she saw. She paid the property tax on the strength of it, and two checks bounced. The fees and the embarrassment kept her awake for a week. She told her pastor she felt foolish and old. The church's tech volunteer, a quiet young woman named Priya, sat down with her the next Sunday afternoon. She helped Mrs. Hayes move the household accounts into the family app the church used, which ran on the church's own equipment and never sold anyone's information. Then Priya showed her the difference that mattered. Every number on the screen traced back to a real record with a real date. When the bank connection had not updated, the app said so plainly, with the time of the last real update, instead of guessing. Mrs. Hayes studied it for a long time. Then she said that was the first piece of software that had ever been honest with her. Over the next year she ran the household carefully and well. She told Priya once that she did not need the machine to be clever. She needed it to be faithful, the way her husband had been, telling her the truth even when the truth was only that it did not know yet.

dsi2-the-shared-data-layer.title: Choir Practice in the Basement
dsi2-the-shared-data-layer.body: The choir at Greater Mount Zion rehearsed in the church basement, where no phone had ever found a signal. For years that meant Sister Antoinette took attendance on a clipboard, then typed it all in upstairs later, and half the time the clipboard got lost under somebody's hymnal. The first Tuesday with the new app, she opened it on her tablet in the basement, half expecting it to spin and give up. It did not. She tapped each singer's name as they came in, marked the songs they worked on, and noted that the tenors needed another pass at the bridge. Everything saved instantly, right there on the tablet. "Where's it going?" asked Deacon Ross, peering over her shoulder. "Nowhere yet," she said. "It's on my tablet for now. When I go upstairs and catch the signal, it'll copy itself up to the church's own storage, and then the choir director will see it on her phone at home." At nine o'clock she climbed the stairs, and by the time she reached the parking lot the little indicator showed everything had synced. The next morning the choir director messaged her a thank-you for the note about the tenors. Antoinette also noticed something. The deacons could see the attendance, but the singers could not see each other's phone numbers, and her granddaughter, who borrowed the tablet for games, could not see a single thing about the choir at all. The app knew who each person was and what they were allowed to open. She told Deacon Ross it felt like a good usher. Quiet, quick, and never letting anyone into a pew that wasn't theirs.

dsi2-the-shared-data-layer.title: The Wall That Cannot Be Walked Around
dsi2-the-shared-data-layer.body: Years before, the family had used a different program to keep track of the household and the rental property. It hid the money pages from the children by simply not showing the buttons. Then one evening their fourteen-year-old, Jonah, curious and clever, changed a few letters in the address bar of the browser and found himself looking at every bank account the family owned, along with the tenants' payment history. He did nothing harmful. He told his mother right away, frightened by what he had found. But she sat awake that night thinking about what a less honest person could have done with the tenants' information, and about how little a hidden button had actually protected. When the family moved to their new app, Jonah's mother asked the person setting it up one question. "What actually stops a child from seeing the money?" The answer was different this time. The protection did not live on the screen at all. It lived inside the database itself, like a guard standing at every drawer, checking two things before opening it: who you are and your relationship to that record. A child's role was denied the money and security records at the database level, row by row. There was no address to change and no button to find, because the drawer simply would not open for him. The tenant downstairs could report a leaking sink and confirm it was fixed, but could never reach a single money record. Jonah, older now, tried his old trick out of curiosity and got nowhere. He grinned and told his mother it was finally a real wall. She said that was the point. Guarding what has been entrusted to you is not suspicion. It is love made structural.

dsi3-the-loops.title: The Chart That Stopped in March
dsi3-the-loops.body: At the October council meeting, Pastor Reid proudly pointed at the attendance chart on the wall screen. It showed a gentle, steady line. Then Mrs. Okonkwo, who never missed a thing, leaned forward and squinted. "Pastor, that line has been exactly the same since March." She was right. The chart had stopped updating seven months earlier, when the greeters switched to a new sign-in sheet that nobody connected to anything. For seven months everyone had glanced at a picture of the past and assumed it was the present. That was the day the church started running loops on purpose. Five steps, over and over. Detect: notice the thing that is wrong, like a line that never moves. Understand: trace it back to the real data before touching anything. They found the old sign-in feed and the new paper sheet that had replaced it. Execute: connect the new sheet properly. Quality control: prove it works, not just believe it. They counted heads by hand on two Sundays and checked that the chart matched both counts exactly. Update: let the live screen show the new, true numbers. Then they did something better. They set up a simple watch on every chart in the system, a note of when real data last flowed through it. If any chart went quiet longer than it should, it would raise its hand and say so, instead of sitting there looking healthy. The next spring, the giving chart went quiet for nine days after a bank change. The system flagged it on day three. Mrs. Okonkwo was delighted. She said she was glad to have some help keeping an eye on things, finally.

dsi3-the-loops.title: Done Is Not a Feeling
dsi3-the-loops.body: Mother Viola's eyes had been failing for years. She read the order of service on the church's app every Sunday, holding her phone almost against her nose. One week a volunteer named Trent redesigned the colors of that page to look more modern, soft gray letters on a pale background. He looked at it on his own bright phone, decided it looked wonderful, and marked the task done. That Sunday Mother Viola could not read a single line. She sat through the service lost, too proud to ask her neighbor what hymn they were on. Her daughter mentioned it to the media team afterward, gently. Trent was crushed. He had not meant any harm. He had simply decided it was done because it felt done. The team lead sat down with him and explained the step he had skipped. "Looking right is not the same as being right," she said. "When we fix something, we prove it." They measured the contrast between the letters and the background with a tool that gives a real number, and it failed the standard by a wide margin. Trent fixed the colors and measured again until the number passed. Then the team added a check that would automatically refuse any page whose contrast fell below the standard, and they tested that check by feeding it Trent's old gray design to make sure it actually caught the problem. It did. The next Sunday Mother Viola read the whole order of service and sang every hymn. Trent watched her from the booth. He told the team lead later that he had learned the most important lesson of his volunteer life. Done is not a feeling. Done is when you can show the proof.

dsi4-how-modules-connect.title: One Recording, Many Baskets
