dsi4-how-modules-connect.body: The first Sunday Malik ran the recording, he forgot to unmute the pulpit microphone for the first twenty minutes. The video was fine, but the sermon's opening was silent. He shrugged. It was only the recording. Then on Monday he saw what that silence cost. The church's system took each recorded service and transcribed it once, turning the audio into text on the church's own machines. From that one transcript, it harvested everything: the sermon went to the archive of messages, the Scripture references went into the Scripture library, the songs the choir sang went to the choir's library linked back to the exact moment in the video, and the teaching points became material for lessons. Because the opening was silent, the transcript began in the middle of the second point. The Scripture library was missing the pastor's main text. The children's lesson writer had nothing to build from. One careless switch had starved six different places downstream. The next Sunday Malik checked every microphone twice before service and watched the audio meters the whole time. On Monday the harvest ran clean. Sister Marguerite, who sang in the alto section, found the song she had led linked right in the choir library, and she sent a clip of it to her grandson. The children's teacher built her lesson from the sermon's own words. The Scripture references sat neatly in the library with the date beside them. Malik realized that he was not just a man pushing record in the back. He was one member of a body, and what he did well at the beginning multiplied into everything that came after.

dsi4-how-modules-connect.title: No Video Lost
dsi4-how-modules-connect.body: The harvest screen at the church listed every recorded service and showed which parts had been gathered from it and which were still gaps. The services with the most missing pieces rose to the top of the list on their own, so nothing could quietly fall to the bottom and be forgotten. One afternoon a volunteer named Helena was working down the list when a service from two winters earlier rose to the top. It had been recorded, but only the sermon had ever been harvested. Out of curiosity she opened the full recording. Near the end, after the sermon, the pastor had invited Brother Ezekiel Moore to share a testimony. He was ninety-one then, and he spoke for eleven minutes about the year his family lost their farm, and how the church had carried them, and how he had come to trust Yahweh in the lean seasons. Brother Moore had gone home to be with Jesus the following spring. His family had searched for any recording of his voice and had been told there was nothing. Helena sat very still. Then she harvested the testimony properly, transcribed it, tagged it, and placed it in the church's record of testimonies with his name and the date. She called his granddaughter that evening. The family gathered the next Sunday after service and watched it together in the fellowship hall. His great-grandson, who had never met him, sat closest to the screen. Helena thought about the baskets of leftovers the disciples gathered after the great crowd was fed. She had not created anything new that day. She had simply refused to let a treasure stay buried in an unharvested recording.

dsi5-meet-ari.title: The Helper Who Said It Might Be Wrong
dsi5-meet-ari.body: Grandma Celestine did not trust computers, and she certainly did not trust one that talked. So when her granddaughter showed her the app's helper, Ari, she folded her arms and decided to test it. She opened the church calendar and asked Ari to explain what was on the screen. Ari explained it plainly: the women's fellowship on Thursday, choir rehearsal Friday, and a note that the Saturday food pantry had no time listed yet. Then it added something Celestine did not expect. It said it was a helper that could make mistakes, and that she should check anything important with the church office. Celestine narrowed her eyes. "Well, at least it's honest." Her granddaughter, Nia, explained a little more. Ari was the same helper everywhere in the app, whether it was tutoring a class or reading a page aloud, so it never changed its personality from one screen to the next. It ran on the church's own computers, so nothing Grandma said to it was being shipped off and sold. And its name meant lion, taken from the Lion of Judah, though Ari itself would never claim to be anything more than a tool that served under Yahweh, the Most High. Celestine thought about that for a while. Then she called the church office to check the pantry time, just as Ari had suggested. It turned out Ari had been right, the time really was missing, and the secretary added it on the spot. Celestine hung up satisfied. She told Nia she might let the helper stay, so long as it kept admitting it was not the one in charge.

dsi5-meet-ari.title: The Woman in the Last Pew
dsi5-meet-ari.body: Sister Pearl had sat in the last pew for thirty-four years. She cleaned the fellowship hall after every funeral and folded every bulletin on Saturday mornings, and almost no one knew her last name. She had never been asked to speak, and she would not have known how to begin. When the church began recording testimonies for its history, the volunteer in charge, Ruth, noticed that every one came from the same few familiar voices. Ruth went looking for the people no one had thought to ask. She found Sister Pearl folding bulletins and asked if she would tell her story. Pearl said she had nothing worth telling. Ruth sat with her anyway. With Pearl's permission, Ruth recorded their conversation on the church's own equipment, where nothing would be sold or shared beyond the church. Afterward the church's A.I. helper, Ari, transcribed it and helped Ruth arrange it, and Ruth checked every word against the recording, because the helper could make mistakes and Pearl's words deserved to be exactly right. It was the story of a young widow who came to the city with nothing, who found a church that fed her children, and who had spent the rest of her life quietly feeding others in return. The next month it played at the women's fellowship. When it ended, the room was silent, and then every woman in it stood. Pearl wept. She told Ruth later that she had felt invisible all her life. Ruth told her gently that she had never been unseen, not for one day. Yahweh is the One who sees. The tools had only helped the rest of them finally catch up.

dsi6-the-nas.title: The Box Nobody Could Find
dsi6-the-nas.body: Wesley, a new volunteer, was sitting in a coffee shop trying to open the church's storage box from his laptop. He typed its address into the browser. Nothing. He tried again. Still nothing. He messaged the team lead, Celia, annoyed. "I think the storage box is broken. I can't reach it from here." Celia's reply came back with a smiling face. "It's not broken. It's working perfectly. That box isn't on the public internet at all, on purpose. Nobody in that coffee shop can reach it, and neither can you, until you connect through our private network." She walked him through joining the church's secure private connection from his laptop. The box appeared instantly. Wesley felt a little foolish, and then a little impressed. "So the reason I couldn't find it," he said, "is the same reason a stranger can't find it." "Exactly," Celia said. "The smallest target is the one that isn't showing." While he was connected, Wesley opened the app's infrastructure page to check how full the drives were. It showed a real reading taken from the box a few minutes earlier, with a timestamp. One service on the page was marked "stale" because it had not reported in an hour, and Celia told him that was precisely why the page was trustworthy. "If it ever told you everything was fine when it didn't actually know, you'd never be able to believe it again." Wesley started to understand that the box in the office was more than a hard drive. It was the barn where the church kept its riches, and the brain that kept the helpers running. And a well-built house, he thought, does not leave its storeroom door open to the street.

dsi6-the-nas.title: Before You Promise
dsi6-the-nas.body: After a storm knocked out power to half the city, the pastor asked his media volunteer, Cedric, a simple question in the hallway. "Our recordings are safe at the church now too, right? The new storage box there?" Cedric almost said yes. He had heard people talk about the church's own storage box for months. It sounded finished. It would have been easy to nod and let the pastor rest easy. But Cedric had learned to check rather than assume, so he said he would confirm and get right back to him. He called the steward who managed the systems. The answer was not what he expected. The home storage box was running and backed up, but the church's own box was still being built. The recordings from the last four months existed in only one place. Cedric felt his stomach drop. He went back to the pastor and told him the truth, plainly: not yet, and here is what we're doing about it. That same afternoon he and the steward copied the most recent recordings to the home box's backup, encrypted and sealed, so there were at least two safe copies while the church's box was finished. He wrote it on the team's board so no one else would assume otherwise. Three weeks later the church's box was complete and tested, and the recordings were finally stored in both places. The pastor stopped Cedric after service one Sunday and thanked him, not for the work, but for the honesty. He said a false yes would have felt kind that day and been cruel later. Cedric thought about Joseph gathering grain before the lean years came. The storehouse only counts if it is truly full.

dsi7-the-gpu-node.title: The Moving Truck
dsi7-the-gpu-node.body: Aaron had just learned that the church had two machines with strong graphics cards, and he was ready to run the biggest A.I. model he could find on them. He downloaded one with seventy billion parameters and watched it refuse to load. He tried again. It refused again. Kezia, who looked after the machines, came over with a picture on her phone of a small pickup truck and a pile of furniture. "This graphics card is a very good truck," she said. "It's fast, and it hauls quickly. That's why we use it to transcribe the recordings instead of the storage box, which would take all night. But everything you want to move has to fit in the truck bed. That model is a whole house of furniture. It needs roughly twice the room this truck has, even packed tight." Aaron asked what the truck could carry. Kezia pulled up the team's notes. A model around fourteen billion parameters fit comfortably, and with careful packing it could stretch toward twenty. "That's our honest envelope," she said. "Inside it, this machine is wonderful. It lets the church's helper think right here in the building, without sending anybody's words to an outside company. Outside it, we'd just be pretending." Aaron sighed and loaded a fourteen-billion model instead. It ran quickly and answered well, and he spent the afternoon testing it on the church's real questions. When a bigger machine came up in the budget later, he was the first to explain to the council exactly why it would matter and what it could carry. Kezia said that was skill put to holy use: knowing what a tool can do, and using it right.

dsi7-the-gpu-node.title: Sacred Hours
dsi7-the-gpu-node.body: The church had two machines with strong graphics cards. One handled the everyday work: the local A.I., the automations, the transcription of recordings. The other ran the live production during services, routing video and putting the lyrics and Scripture on the screen. The rule for that second machine was simple and firm. During church hours, it ran nothing but worship. No A.I. jobs, no transcriptions, no updates, nothing that could slow it down. One Sunday morning a new volunteer named Bryce noticed that the everyday machine was busy and the production machine seemed to have spare capacity. He was trying to help. He started a large transcription job on the production machine at ten forty, just before the service. At eleven fifteen, in the middle of a hushed prayer, the lyrics on the screen froze, then skipped, then went dark for four long seconds. The worship leader carried on, and the congregation followed, but Bryce felt sick in the booth. He stopped the job at once, and the screens recovered. Afterward the team lead, Simeon, did not shame him. He sat with him and explained why the line existed. Those machines were tools made with real skill, and every tool has a purpose. The purpose of the production machine on Sunday morning was to serve a room full of people meeting Yahweh, and nothing else was allowed to compete with that. Bryce asked if he could write the rule on a card and tape it to the machine. Simeon said yes. The card still hangs there, in Bryce's careful handwriting. No other work during service. The room comes first. Bryce now teaches it to every new volunteer himself.

dsi8-the-led-wall.title: The Two Lanes
dsi8-the-led-wall.body: At seven thirty on a Sunday morning, Darnell plugged the network video cable from the camera system straight into the box that drives the big LED wall, and nothing happened. The wall stayed black. He tried a different port. Black. He tried restarting the box. Still black. Choir members were filing in and glancing at the dark wall, and Darnell was starting to sweat. Mrs. Abernathy, the media lead, arrived, took one look, and laughed kindly. "Two lanes, baby," she said. She pulled out a whiteboard marker and drew it on the back of a bulletin. One lane was the wall lane: the presentation computer sends the picture through a video cable, into the wall's processor, and onto the wall. The other lane was the network lane: the cameras and production feeds travel around the building's network to the switcher, the stream, and the side screens. "The wall's processor has no door for network video," she said. "If you want a network picture on the wall, you have to turn it into a video cable signal first. Different lanes, different roads." She plugged the presentation computer's video cable into the processor's high-bandwidth input, and the wall glowed to life, sharp from edge to edge, with three minutes to spare. Darnell kept that bulletin. That week he drew the two lanes cleanly on a card, labeled every port on the processor, and taped the card to the media desk. The next volunteer who got confused at seven thirty in the morning did not even need to call anyone. She read the card, plugged in the right cable, and the wall came up on the first try. Plain, written down, and ready for the next person.

dsi8-the-led-wall.title: Mother's Face on the Wall
dsi8-the-led-wall.body: When Mother Gwendolyn Bryant passed at ninety-three, her family asked the church to put her photograph on the big LED wall during the homegoing service. Her grandson sent over a picture taken from his phone, a small square image he had cropped from a family reunion. The media volunteer, Esther, put it up to test it the night before. On the great wall, the little square picture stretched sideways into a blurry, swollen face that hardly looked like Mother Bryant at all. The wall was so fine and sharp that it showed every soft edge without mercy. Esther took it down at once. She called the grandson and asked, gently, whether anyone had an original photograph. His aunt had one, a formal portrait from Mother Bryant's eightieth birthday, printed and framed. Esther drove to the aunt's house that evening and borrowed it. At the church she scanned it at the highest resolution the scanner allowed. Then she placed it on a background the wall's exact size and shape, widescreen and edge to edge, so nothing would be stretched or squeezed. She tested it on the wall again near midnight. This time Mother Bryant looked out at the empty sanctuary as clearly as if she were standing at the front, her familiar smile, the pearl earrings she wore every Sunday, her eyes bright and kind. During the service, her daughter looked up at the wall and covered her mouth with both hands. Afterward she found Esther and said that her mother looked like herself, and that it had been a comfort to see her honored that way. Esther thought that some work is done best when it is done carefully enough for no one to notice.

dsi9-sunday-and-wednesday.title: The Wednesday Walk-Through
dsi9-sunday-and-wednesday.body: Every new volunteer at Bethany started the same way: on a quiet Wednesday afternoon, walking the whole building with Mr. Augustine, who had served on the tech team for twenty years. He called it following the river. They started at the presentation computer. "This is where the words begin," he said. "Lyrics, Scripture, the announcements. They go out through this cable, into the wall's processor, and onto the big wall. That's the first lane." Then he led them to the cameras. "These pictures don't use a cable to the wall. They travel the network, to the switcher that chooses what goes out, to the stream for the folks at home, and to the two side screens. That's the second lane." He pointed to a machine humming in the corner. "That one can transcribe the service and run our helper, but only when the room isn't using it. During service, worship gets everything." Last, he walked them to the office and showed them a list of services from past Sundays. "And here's the part people forget. After the last amen, the recording keeps working. One good recording becomes the sermon archive, the Scripture library, the choir's songs, and the lessons. If you capture it well on Sunday, it feeds the church all week." A new volunteer named Rhea asked why they had to learn all of it if she was only going to run slides. Mr. Augustine smiled. "Because you're not just running slides. You're one part of the wall, and the wall only goes up when every one of us works it with one heart." Rhea ran slides that Sunday, and she knew exactly where her words were going.

dsi9-sunday-and-wednesday.title: Not on Easter
dsi9-sunday-and-wednesday.body: The new presentation software was beautiful. It ran in a browser, needed no graphics card, and would free up the production machine for other work. Several volunteers wanted to switch to it in time for Easter, the biggest Sunday of the year. Ingrid, who led the media team, said no. She did not say it lightly. She liked the new software too. But she had seen what happens when untested tools meet a full sanctuary. Years earlier, at another church, she had watched a brand-new system fail in the middle of a Christmas service, the screen turning glaring white during the most solemn hymn, the operator frantically restarting while the congregation stood confused. She would not gamble live worship on something unproven. So she laid out a plan instead. The new software would run alongside the old one for eight Sundays, on a separate screen, showing the same cues, while the old system stayed in charge. It had to prove four things: that it never showed a white screen, that it recovered instantly from a crash, that it fell back to a calm holding slide if a cue was broken, and that it worked through real services without a single surprise. Some volunteers grumbled about waiting. Easter came and went on the old system, without a hitch. By the sixth Sunday the new software had passed every test, including one rough morning when the volunteer deliberately unplugged it mid-song to see what would happen. It came back in two seconds, right where it had been. On the ninth Sunday, it took over. No one in the pews noticed the change at all, which was exactly what Ingrid had prayed for. Order, she said, is how you protect people who came to worship.

dsi10-running-a-service.title: One Step Ahead
dsi10-running-a-service.body: Hazel's first three Sundays running the presentation were a chase. The worship leader would start the chorus, and Hazel would still be hunting for it. The congregation would be halfway through the second verse before the right words appeared on the wall. By the third Sunday she was exhausted and convinced she was not cut out for it. Brother Lucius, who had run presentation for years, invited her to come in on Saturday afternoon. "Most of this job happens before anybody walks in," he said. They built the set together. Each song with its sections in the order the team would actually sing them, verse, chorus, verse, chorus, bridge, chorus. The Scripture passages, checked against the pastor's notes. The announcements. Each image sized for the wall so it would look sharp. Then he taught her the real skill. "When the leader starts a section, you already have the next one ready. You're not reacting. You're one step ahead, listening for where the song is going." On Sunday Hazel sat with her set ready and her finger resting on the next cue. When the leader drew a breath before the chorus, the chorus was already on the wall. When the pastor said, turn with me, the passage was already up. She stopped chasing and started listening. By the end of the service she realized she had actually worshiped, singing along under her breath while she worked. Afterward the worship leader found her and said the words had been right there all morning, like she could read his mind. Hazel laughed and said she just did her homework on Saturday. Brother Lucius said that is what diligence looks like.

dsi10-running-a-service.title: The Holding Slide
dsi10-running-a-service.body: It happened during the quietest moment of the morning. The pastor had asked the congregation to bow for a time of silent prayer, and Josephine, running the presentation, sent the next cue: a simple image of an open Bible. Instead of the image, the output flickered and went to a plain dark slide with the church's name softly in the corner. Something in the cue had broken. Two years earlier, on the old system, a moment like this would have meant a glaring white screen over the whole sanctuary, and Josephine would have panicked, clicked everything, and made it worse. She had done exactly that once, and she still remembered the heat in her face. But she had learned since then. The new system was built so that a broken cue fell back to a calm holding slide instead of white, and so that if it crashed and she reloaded, it would return her to the same place in seconds. Because she knew those safety nets were there, she did not flail. She took a breath. She left the holding slide up, because it was dark and quiet and no one in prayer was disturbed by it. She found the image, saw that the file had been saved in the wrong format, and replaced it with the backup copy she kept in the set. Then she waited for the pastor to lift his head before sending anything new. Nobody in the room knew anything had gone wrong. Afterward the team lead asked her how she had stayed so calm. Josephine said she had prepared the set as if Yahweh were the only one watching, and she trusted the work she had done before the trouble came.

dsi11-adding-content-no-json.title: Grandma Lucille's Pound Cake
dsi11-adding-content-no-json.body: Grandma Lucille had been asked for her pound cake recipe so many times that she finally agreed to put it in the church's app. Then she spent a week refusing to touch the app, because she was sure she would break it. Her grandson Marcus offered to do it for her. She refused that too. "If it's my recipe, I'm putting it in myself," she said. So on a Sunday afternoon Marcus sat beside her at the kitchen table with the tablet. He showed her where the church's kitchen corner was and the button to add a new recipe. A plain form appeared with a box for the name, a box for the ingredients, a box for the steps, and a place for a photo. Lucille stared at it suspiciously. "That's it? No codes? No special language?" "That's it, Grandma. You just type it like you'd write it on a card." She typed slowly with one finger, reading each line out loud. Two cups of sugar. A pound of butter, softened, not melted, and she typed that part in capital letters. Six eggs. When she finished, she held her breath and tapped save. The recipe appeared at once in the kitchen corner, with her name beneath it. Marcus explained that it was saved for real now, stored with the church's other recipes and showing up for anyone in the church who opened the app. That evening, three people from the choir messaged her to say they had found it. One asked whether the butter really mattered that much. Lucille replied that it mattered more than anything. She told Marcus later that giving had never been so easy, and that she might add her sweet potato pie next.

dsi11-adding-content-no-json.title: The Song for Her Husband
dsi11-adding-content-no-json.body: Sister Delores wanted one thing for the first anniversary of her husband's passing: for the choir to sing the old hymn he had loved, the one he hummed every morning while he made coffee. Under the church's old system, adding a song to the service meant emailing the music director, who emailed the office, who typed it into a spreadsheet, who sent it to the person who made the slides. Somewhere in that chain the year before, her request had gotten lost, and the song had not been sung at his memorial. She had never said anything about it, but it had hurt. This year her niece showed her the church's new app. Delores was hesitant. She was not good with technology, she said, and she did not want to make a mess of anything. Her niece opened the choir songbook and handed her the phone. Delores searched for the hymn by name, and there it was. She tapped once to add it to the coming Sunday's service, with a short note to the director about why. That was all. The request went straight to the real order of service, where the director, the choir, and the person running the slides could all see it. The next morning the director called her personally to say the choir would be honored to sing it. On Sunday, when the choir began the first verse, Delores closed her eyes and could almost smell the coffee. Afterward she thanked her niece through tears. She said it was the simplest thing in the world, and that a willing heart should never have to fight a machine just to bring its gift to the house of worship.

dsi12-voice-and-help.title: The Question Mark
dsi12-voice-and-help.body: Mr. Theodore Banks had been staring at the volunteer schedule screen for fifteen minutes. He was supposed to sign up for usher duty in March. He could see March. He could see his name. He could not, for the life of him, figure out how to put the two together. He was too proud to call his daughter for the third time that week. Then he noticed the little question mark in the corner of the screen. He had seen it before and assumed it was for young people. With a sigh, he tapped it. A short explanation appeared, in plain words, telling him what the screen was for, how to sign up for a date, and why the schedule mattered to the people counting on him. At the bottom was a button that said "Hear this." He tapped that too, and the explanation read itself aloud to him in a calm voice while he followed along with his finger. Within a minute he had signed up for two Sundays in March. Feeling bold, he tried another button, "Talk about this." The helper described what was actually on his screen right then: that he was signed up for the second and fourth Sundays, and that the first Sunday still needed two ushers. He signed up for that one too. His daughter called that evening to ask if he needed help with the schedule. Theodore told her, with great satisfaction, that he had handled it himself. She asked how. He admitted he had finally asked for help, just not from her. He told her there was a lot less shame in asking when the help was patient and always right there waiting.

dsi12-voice-and-help.title: See and Hear
dsi12-voice-and-help.body: Sister Marjorie had taught Sunday school for forty-one years. When glaucoma took most of her sight, she stopped coming to the Tuesday Bible study, because she could no longer read the handouts or the lesson on the screen, and she could not bear to keep asking the person beside her to read aloud. The church's youth leader, a young man named Andre, noticed her absence and drove over to see her. He brought a tablet. He sat beside her and turned the app's text size up as large as it would go, until each word filled most of the line. Then he showed her the button that said "Read this page," and the tablet read the week's lesson aloud to her, word for word. Marjorie sat very still and listened. Then he showed her one more thing, "Talk about this." When she tapped it, the app's helper explained what was on the screen in plain language: the passage, the questions for discussion, and the time and place of the study. Andre told her one more thing he thought she would appreciate. The helper was built so that it could not make up a number or a fact that was not really on the screen. If it tried, a guard would stop it. "It only tells you what's there," he said. "Nothing invented." Marjorie said that was more than she could say for some people. The next Tuesday she was back at the study, the tablet in her lap, listening with a small earphone. When the discussion began, she was the first to answer. She told Andre afterward that she had not realized how much help she had been missing, and that she had not felt this capable in years.

dsi13-roles-and-permissions.title: The Missing Buttons
dsi13-roles-and-permissions.body: Cheryl had volunteered in the church office for three weeks when she leaned over to her friend Tamika's screen and gasped. Tamika had tabs Cheryl did not have. A whole section for the order of service. A section for the choir. Buttons for editing announcements. Cheryl went back to her own screen and looked again. None of it was there. "I think my app is broken," she said, a little hurt. "Or I did something wrong when I signed in." Tamika laughed and shook her head. "Nothing's broken. I'm a steward. I run the operations, so I can change those pages. You're helping with the visitor follow-up, so your screen has exactly what that job needs." She showed Cheryl her own screen properly. Cheryl had the visitor cards, the follow-up list, and the notes. That was her work, and it was all there. "So I can't mess up the order of service even if I tried?" Cheryl asked. "Not a chance. It isn't hidden from you. You just don't have that job, so the system won't let you write to it." Cheryl thought about that and felt something unexpected. Relief. She had spent three weeks being careful not to touch the wrong thing. Now she knew she could not touch the wrong thing, because the wrong things were not hers. She could do her own work with her whole heart and stop worrying about everyone else's. When the pastor asked her a month later whether she wanted more access, she asked what responsibilities came with it first. Tamika later told the pastor that was exactly the kind of person who should have it.

dsi13-roles-and-permissions.title: The Ceiling That Cannot Be Raised
dsi13-roles-and-permissions.body: Naomi was a single mother who worked two jobs, and her seven-year-old son, Elijah, used her tablet almost every evening while she cooked. She loved that he could read Bible stories in the family app and do his lessons there. But she lay awake some nights worrying about everything else on that tablet. The household money. The bank connections. The security settings for their apartment. One wrong tap from a curious little boy could cause real damage, and she could not watch him every minute. When she finally asked the church's tech volunteer about it, he explained something that let her sleep. Elijah's account was set up as a child, and the limits on a child's role were not just hidden buttons. They were built into the data itself. A child was locked out of finances, spending, and security entirely, with a hard ceiling that could not be raised, not by accident, and not on purpose by anyone. "Even if you wanted to give him access to the money," the volunteer said, "the system wouldn't let you. It doesn't depend on you remembering to be careful." Naomi tested it herself, logged in as Elijah, and tried everything she could think of. Every money page simply refused to open. She cried a little in the church parking lot afterward, from relief more than anything. Months later the church asked her to become a steward for the children's ministry, with more access than she had ever had. She accepted, but she took it soberly. She knew now how much protection those walls gave to the little ones, and she understood that being trusted with more meant being responsible for more.

dsi14-your-onboarding-path.title: Hours, Not Weeks
dsi14-your-onboarding-path.body: When Felicia joined the tech team at her church, she expected what happened at her last job: weeks of shadowing someone, trying to remember a hundred things they mentioned once, and feeling lost every Sunday. Instead, the team lead sent her a link to a course inside the church's own app. She opened it on a Thursday evening with a cup of tea, half expecting to give up after an hour. It started with the simplest question, what the app actually was, and then moved step by step: where the data lived, how the improvement loops worked, how the pieces connected, the storage box, the graphics machines, the big wall, and finally the skills, running a service, adding content, using the help, knowing her role. At the end of each module there was a short quiz. She failed the first one on the data layer, reread the section, and passed it the second time. By Saturday afternoon she had finished every module and earned a completion record that showed her real scores, not a pretend gold star. On Sunday morning she walked into the booth and knew what every machine did. When the presentation computer hiccupped, she knew it would fall back to a holding slide. When a new volunteer asked why the wall would not take the network video, Felicia drew the two lanes on a bulletin without thinking. The team lead watched her and grinned. Afterward, Felicia asked if she could help improve the course for the next person. She had found one section that could be clearer. The team lead said that was exactly how the course was meant to grow, trained by the people who walked it first.

dsi14-your-onboarding-path.title: To Confirm
dsi14-your-onboarding-path.body: Halfway through the onboarding course, Marcus reached a section on the sound system with a small note in plain words: this setting is to confirm with the sound engineer. At his old church, he would have guessed. He had seen people guess before. Years earlier the man who knew the sound board best had moved away suddenly, taking everything in his head with him, and the volunteers left behind spent two years guessing their way through Sunday mornings, feedback squealing, microphones dropping out, the pastor straining to be heard. They had never written anything down, and they had never asked, because there was no one left to ask. So when Marcus saw the note, he did something simple. He found the sound engineer after service and asked. The engineer was surprised and pleased. He spent forty minutes walking Marcus through why that setting mattered and what happened when it was wrong. Then he said he would update the course himself so the next person would not need to ask. Marcus was struck by that. The course was not a dead manual. It drew from the same help that the app's question mark showed, so when the engineer fixed it, it was fixed everywhere at once. And it was honest about its own edges. Where it did not know something for certain, it said so, and pointed to the person who did. A year later Marcus was the one new volunteers came to with questions. He always answered the same way: here is what I know, and here is who knows more. He told the team lead it was the difference between knowledge that leaves with a person and knowledge that is handed on.

aib1-the-one-rule.title: The Billboard Test
aib1-the-one-rule.body: Keisha was fourteen and upset. Her best friend had said something unkind at lunch. Now Keisha sat at the kitchen table typing the whole story into a free chatbot app. She typed her friend's full name. She typed the names of three other girls. She even typed a secret her friend had once told her. She wanted the chatbot to say who was right. Nana Ruth was shelling peas across the table. "Who are you telling all that to?" "Nobody," Keisha said. "It's just the A.I." Nana Ruth set the peas down. "That's not nobody. That's a stranger's computer far away. They can keep what you type. Sometimes people there read it. Pressing delete does not promise it's gone." She pointed out the window. "See that big billboard by the highway? Would you want every word you just typed up on that sign, with your friend's name ten feet tall?" Keisha looked at her phone for a long time. Then she erased every line without sending it. She asked a new question with no names at all: how do you talk to a friend who hurt your feelings? The answer helped. That night she called her friend, and they made up. Nana Ruth smiled. One rule, she said, is enough.

aib1-the-one-rule.title: Delete Is Not Gone
aib1-the-one-rule.body: In the hardest season of his life, Harold could not sleep. His marriage was in trouble, and he felt too ashamed to call anyone. So late one night he opened a free chatbot and typed everything. His wife's name. His children's names. Their fights. Their money troubles. A private matter only the two of them knew. He typed for two hours. In the morning he felt sick about it. He pressed delete and told himself it was gone. Months later, he and his wife were meeting with their pastor and slowly healing. One Sunday a teacher at church explained how chatbots really work. The company keeps what you type on its own computers. Workers may read some of it. It can be used to train the machine. And delete does not promise it is erased. Harold sat in the back row with his face burning. He could not take it back. He could only stop, and tell the truth. That night he told his wife. She was hurt, and then she forgave him. Together they decided that their family's private things would be spoken to Yahweh in prayer, and to trusted people face to face. Now Harold teaches the one rule to the young men at church.

aib2-do-not-share-list.title: The List on the Refrigerator
aib2-do-not-share-list.body: After the church lesson, Grace wrote nine words on a card and stuck it to the refrigerator. Identity. ID numbers. Money. Health. Passwords. Work secrets. Lawyer. Other people. Children. Underneath, in red, she wrote: Never into a chatbot. Her husband, Curtis, thought it was a bit much. Two days later he sat at the counter, trying to get a chatbot to help with the budget. His bank statement was open, and he was about to paste the whole thing in. Their nine-year-old, Benji, walked by for a juice box. He looked at the screen. He looked at the refrigerator. "Dad," he said. "Number three." Curtis turned around. Benji was pointing at the word Money. Curtis laughed so hard he nearly spilled his coffee. Then he closed the statement. He asked the chatbot a general question instead: how can a family split its money between bills, saving, and giving? The answer was useful, and Curtis filled in the real numbers himself, on paper. That week Benji made himself the list inspector. He stopped his sister from pasting her friend's address. Number eight. He stopped Grandma from typing her medicine list. Number four. Grace said those were the nine most useful words she ever wrote.

aib2-do-not-share-list.title: The Widow's Statement
aib2-do-not-share-list.body: Deacon Raymond helped Sister Evelyn with her money after her husband died. She trusted him with everything. Her bank statements. Her account numbers. Her Social Security letters. One evening Raymond sat at his desk, tired and behind. He thought of a shortcut. He could paste her statements into a free chatbot and ask it to sort her spending. It would save an hour. He had already pasted the first page, with her name, address, and account number at the top, when he stopped. He remembered the list from church. Money. Identity. Other people's information. This was all three at once, and none of it was his. Sister Evelyn had given it to him to keep, not to send to a stranger's company far away. He closed the window without sending it. He sat there a while, ashamed of how close he had come and how ordinary it had felt. Then he did the work by hand, with a pencil and a ledger, the slow way. On Sunday he told her what he had almost done. She patted his hand and thanked him for telling the truth. Raymond said keeping a trust means keeping it even when no one would ever know. Sister Evelyn said that was why she chose him.

aib3-how-the-machine-remembers.title: The Switch That Wasn't an Eraser
aib3-how-the-machine-remembers.body: Uncle Frank was proud of himself. He had found the setting in his chatbot app that stops the company from using his chats to train its machine. He turned it off. At Sunday dinner he told everyone that now his chats were private and everything he ever typed was erased. His niece Amara set down her fork. "Uncle Frank, that was a good thing to do. But it doesn't erase anything." He frowned. "I turned it off." "It mostly stops them from using what you type from now on," she said. "It doesn't promise to delete what they already kept. And most of them still hold recent chats for a while anyway." Frank looked let down. "So what's the point?" "It's better," Amara said. "But the bigger thing is what kind of account you have. At my job, we pay for a business version with a written contract. It promises not to train on our words. Your free account is the leaky one. Same name on the door, different rules inside." Frank went quiet. Then he admitted he had been writing letters for his plumbing business with customers' names in them. That week Amara helped him set up the right kind of account. She told him the rules change often, so check the real policy.

aib3-how-the-machine-remembers.title: Counting the Cost of Free
aib3-how-the-machine-remembers.body: Mrs. Adaeze ran a small tax business from her home. For twenty years her clients trusted her with their incomes, their debts, and their Social Security numbers. When chatbots became popular, a young relative showed her how to paste client details into a free account to write letters faster. For one busy season, she did it. It saved her hours. Then she went to a workshop at church. She learned that on a free account, what she typed was stored on the company's computers. Workers might read some of it. It might be used to train the machine. Turning off training usually stopped only future use. And business versions came with real contracts that promised much more. She drove home in silence. That night she sat at her kitchen table and counted the cost honestly. Free had never been free. Her clients had paid for it with their privacy, and no one had asked them. The next morning she stopped using the free account for client work. She paid for a properly contracted tool for the few jobs that needed it, and she did the rest by hand. Then she wrote her clients a letter telling them what she had changed and why. Several called to thank her. None of them left.

aib4-the-law-plain.title: The Lawyer's Letter
aib4-the-law-plain.body: Mr. Otis got a long, confusing letter from his lawyer about his late brother's property. He read it three times and still did not understand it. His grandson said, "Just paste it into a chatbot, Grandpa. It will explain it." Otis was about to do it when his daughter Lena came in with groceries. She worked in a law office. "Daddy, wait," she said. "I'm not a lawyer, and this isn't legal advice. But don't. That letter is private between you and your lawyer, and that privacy helps protect you. If you hand it to an outside company, you could lose that protection." Otis squinted. "It's just a computer." "It's a company's computer," Lena said. "Sharing with them can count like sharing with anybody. It's the same with health records and work secrets. The protection people expect doesn't follow their papers into those apps." Otis set the letter down. "Then how do I understand it?" Lena handed him his phone. "Call your lawyer. That's what he's for." Otis grumbled, but he called. The lawyer spent twenty patient minutes explaining every paragraph. He even said he was glad Otis had not shared it anywhere. That night Otis told his grandson that the smart thing is to stop and find out first, and to ask a real lawyer when it matters.

aib4-the-law-plain.title: The Night Shift Notes
aib4-the-law-plain.body: Nurse Celeste worked nights at a small clinic. At three in the morning she still had a dozen patient notes to finish. A coworker had told her a free chatbot could clean up notes in seconds. Celeste opened it on her own phone and began to copy in the first note. The patient's name. Her birthday. Her illness. Her medicines. Then Celeste stopped. She remembered her training. The law protects patient information when the clinic handles it, or a company that has signed a special promise to protect it. A free chatbot had signed nothing. Pasting the note there would carry it outside every protection the law gave it, and outside the promise the clinic made to every patient. Celeste thought of the frightened grandmother behind that note, who had trusted her only hours before. She deleted the text without sending it. She finished the notes by hand, long after her shift should have ended. The next week she told her supervisor, who thanked her and set up a proper tool with the right agreement. Celeste did not feel brave. She simply believed the laws that protect people are worth keeping, even at three in the morning with no one watching. Keeping them, she told a young nurse, is one way she loves her patients.

aib5-real-world-scenarios.title: The Thank-You List
aib5-real-world-scenarios.body: The volunteer banquet was two weeks away. Sister Bernadette had promised to make a thank-you card for every volunteer, all two hundred and forty of them. She had the church directory open on her laptop, with every name, address, phone number, and birthday. Then she had an idea. She would paste the whole directory into a chatbot and ask it to write a note for each person. She had the list selected when her friend Gloria looked over. "Bernie, is that the whole directory?" "It'll save me a week," Bernadette said. Gloria set down the envelopes. "That's every family in the church. If you paste that in, you give everyone's information to a stranger's company in one click." Bernadette stopped. It had felt like a kindness. She had not seen it that way. Gloria named three safe ways. Do the task without uploading the list. Use the church's own A.I., which stays in the building. Or write the notes by hand. Bernadette chose the first. She asked the chatbot, with no names at all, for twenty warm thank-you messages. She picked her favorites and wrote each name herself with her best pen. It took four evenings instead of one. At the banquet, several volunteers said the handwriting made them cry.

aib5-real-world-scenarios.title: The Get-Well Card
aib5-real-world-scenarios.body: When Brother Lionel became seriously ill, the care ministry wanted to send him a card from the whole church. Yolanda led the ministry, and she sat down to write it. But she had known him for thirty years, and the words would not come. So she opened a chatbot and began to type. His full name. His age. His exact illness. His treatment plan. How hard it was for his wife. She had typed almost all of it when she stopped and read it back. Every word was someone else's private health news. His wife had shared it with her quietly in the church hallway. None of it was Yolanda's to hand to a company far away. It had felt harmless. It had even felt loving. But it was exactly what the church lesson had warned about. Yolanda deleted it all. Then she bowed her head at the kitchen table and asked Yahweh for the words she could not find. After a few quiet minutes she picked up a pen instead of the laptop. She wrote a simple note with no illness and no details. She wrote that the church loved him, that they prayed for him by name, and that he was not alone. His wife said he kept that card by his bed through every week of treatment.

aib6-safe-use-blueprint-sovereign.title: Person A and XXXX
aib6-safe-use-blueprint-sovereign.body: Monique needed help writing a letter to her landlord. The water heater had been broken for three weeks. She remembered the church lesson, so she followed the card step by step. First, she redacted. Instead of her name, she wrote Person A. Instead of the landlord's name, Person B. She left out her address. Instead of her account number, she wrote XXXX. She even left out her street and the month she moved in, because small details can add up to one person. Then she asked a plain question: how should a tenant write a polite, clear letter about a repair that is three weeks late? The chatbot gave her a good draft. She copied it into her own computer and filled in the real names and dates herself, offline. The letter worked. The water heater was fixed that week. Her son Jordan, who was twelve, watched her and asked why she went to all that trouble. Monique showed him the card. Redact first. Never paste passwords. Match the tool to how private the thing is. Turn off what you can. "Be smart about where your words go," she said, "and gentle with other people's. You can use the tool and still keep what's yours." Jordan copied the card for his backpack.

aib6-safe-use-blueprint-sovereign.title: The Benevolence Room
aib6-safe-use-blueprint-sovereign.body: Families came to Deaconess Hattie when they could not pay rent or buy medicine. In a small room off the fellowship hall, they told her everything. Their income. Their debts. Their health. Their children's names. For years she kept it all in a locked cabinet. As the requests grew, she fell behind. Someone told her to use a free chatbot to write the letters. Hattie had been to the church's A.I. class, and she refused. She would not put any family's hardest moment on a stranger's computer. Then the tech team offered another way. The church ran its own A.I. on its own machines, inside its own building. Nothing typed into it ever left. No company kept it. No stranger read it. There was simply no one outside to hand it to. Hattie tested it for a month, checking every summary against her own notes, because it could still make mistakes. Then she began to use it, and she caught up within weeks. Every family's story stayed home. Before Hattie retired, she trained a young woman named Ruthanne. She taught her the billboard rule first, then the whole card. Then she told her the training was not finished until Ruthanne taught it to someone else. That spring, Ruthanne taught the youth group.

wo1-one-upload-everywhere.title: Monday Mornings
wo1-one-upload-everywhere.body: For six years, Mrs. Johnetta Pratt spent every Monday morning the same way. She came into the church office, made her coffee, and opened the old website. She found Sunday's video on the church's channel, copied its code, pasted it into the top of the page in place of last week's, saved it, checked it, and fixed whatever had gone crooked. Then she opened the archive page and added a new button if a month had turned over. On a good Monday it took forty minutes. On a bad one, when the page editor misbehaved, it took the whole morning. Then the church moved to its new app. The volunteer who set it up explained it in a sentence. "Mrs. Pratt, the app reads the channel by itself. When the service streams, the newest message shows up at the top of the church page, and in the recent streams, and in the archive with its date. You don't have to move anything." Johnetta did not believe him. That Sunday, after the service ended, she sat in her kitchen and opened the app on her phone. There was the morning's message at the top, already playing. She scrolled down. It was in the archive too, under the right month, with the right date. On Monday morning she came into the office, made her coffee, and sat down at the computer out of habit. Then she realized there was nothing to do. She laughed out loud. The one job now was simply getting the video onto the channel, and the stream did that on its own. She spent the forty minutes calling three shut-ins instead. She has done it every Monday since.

wo1-one-upload-everywhere.title: Last Week's Sermon
wo1-one-upload-everywhere.body: Brother Calvin Hughes was homebound after his second stroke. His daughter set up the church website on a tablet by his recliner so he could hear the pastor preach each week. But the website was updated by hand, and the volunteer who did it was often busy, sometimes for weeks at a time. Many Sundays Brother Hughes tapped the video at the top of the page and found himself listening to last week's sermon again, or the one from the week before. He never complained. He would just listen to it again, faithfully, because it was what he had. One Sunday in late winter, the pastor preached on the very passage Brother Hughes had asked him to preach on during a hospital visit. The old website did not show it for nineteen days. By then Brother Hughes had been hospitalized again. His daughter played it for him from her phone in the hospital room, and he wept, and he said he wished he had heard it the day it was preached. When the church moved to its new app, the young man who built it heard that story from Brother Hughes's daughter, and it settled into him like a stone. Now the newest message appears at the top of the church page on its own, within minutes of the stream ending. Nobody has to remember to move it. Brother Hughes, home again, opens the tablet every Sunday afternoon and finds that morning's message waiting for him, the same day it was preached. He told the pastor that the Word had always gone out faithfully from the pulpit. Now it finally arrived at his recliner on time.

wo2-find-and-share.title: The Message on Patience
wo2-find-and-share.body: Twelve-year-old Isaiah came home from school frustrated with his little brother, and his grandmother, Mother Lavern, said, "Baby, you need that message the pastor preached on patience." Isaiah asked which one. She did not remember the date. It was sometime last year, maybe in the spring, maybe on a Wednesday night. Under the old website, that would have meant an afternoon of clicking through month buttons and guessing. Instead Mother Lavern opened the Word tab in the church's app on her phone. She typed patience into the search box, and four messages came up. She tapped the filter for Wednesday services, and that narrowed it to one, from April. There it was, the title, the date, and a watch button right beside it. She played the first minute to be sure it was the right one. It was. Then she tapped share and sent the link to Isaiah's tablet. He tapped it, and it opened right to that message, no account, no sign-in, no searching. He watched the whole thing at the kitchen table while she started supper. When it ended, he went and found his little brother and apologized for yelling. Mother Lavern pretended not to notice. Later that week Isaiah's friend from school asked him why he was being so calm lately. Isaiah opened the app, found the same message in about five seconds, and shared it with him too. His grandmother told the pastor about it on Sunday. She said it was the first time she had ever seen one generation hand a sermon to the next by tapping a button.

wo2-find-and-share.title: A Link Across the Country
wo2-find-and-share.body: Mr. Leonard Oduya had not spoken to his son in four years. A hard argument, followed by silence, followed by the slow habit of not calling. His son lived two thousand miles away now and had a child Leonard had seen only in a photograph. One Wednesday night the pastor preached on fathers and sons and the long road home, and Leonard sat in the back pew unable to breathe. He wanted his son to hear it. He did not know how to say any of it himself. On Sunday he asked the young woman who ran the church's media how he could send a message to someone who did not belong to the church and would never sign up for anything. She showed him the Word tab in the app. She found the Wednesday message by its date, tapped share, and explained that whoever received the link would land right on that message, on any phone or computer, without needing an account to watch it. Leonard went home and stared at his phone for an hour. Then he sent the link with only four words. I've been thinking. Dad. Three days passed with no reply. On the fourth, his phone rang. His son's voice was thick. He said he had watched the message twice, once alone and once with his wife. They talked for an hour that night, and for an hour the next week, and in the summer Leonard met his grandson for the first time. He told the pastor afterward that he had been trying for four years to find the words. In the end, he had only needed to share the ones already preached.

wo3-retire-the-old-site.title: The Last Edit
wo3-retire-the-old-site.body: Tremaine had inherited the church's old website along with a list of instructions from the last volunteer. Every month: replace the featured video, add a month button to the archive page, check that nothing broke. He hated it. The page editor was slow, the buttons never lined up, and the moment a new service was streamed, the page was already out of date again. When the church launched its new app, the pastor asked whether the old site could stay up a while for people who still had it bookmarked. Tremaine sighed, thinking that meant monthly busywork forever. Then the app's builder showed him one simple change. Instead of pasting a single video into the old page, he could paste in the channel's uploads playlist. That playlist always put the newest video first on its own. One edit, and the old page would show the latest message forever, without anyone touching it again. Tremaine made the change on a Tuesday afternoon. It took six minutes. Then he did one more thing. He removed the long column of month buttons, because the Word tab in the app already sorted every message by month automatically, and he added a clear line at the top of the old page: the church's home is now the app, with a link to it. The next Sunday, the old site showed the new message the moment the stream ended. So did the app. Tremaine deleted the monthly instructions from his phone with great ceremony. His wife asked what he was going to do with his free Saturday mornings. He said he was going to come to the men's breakfast for the first time in a year.

wo3-retire-the-old-site.title: A Time to Set It Down
wo3-retire-the-old-site.body: For eleven years, Deacon Marvin Ellis kept the church's old website. He was not a technical man. He had taught himself how to paste in each Sunday's video and build the archive one month button at a time, sitting at his kitchen table late on Sunday nights. Hundreds of buttons, each one made by hand. He was quietly proud of it. Some months it was the only service he felt able to give. So when the church moved to its new app, which did all of it automatically, Marvin felt something he did not have words for. Relief, but also loss. The work of his hands was about to be retired. The young woman who built the app understood. She asked him to sit with her and make the last edit together. She showed him how to replace the single pasted video with the channel's playlist, so the old page would always show the newest message from then on, without him. Marvin made the change himself, slowly, with her beside him. Then together they took down the month buttons, one column at a time. When it was done, she asked the pastor to say something on Sunday. He did. He told the congregation that for eleven years, every sermon they had found online, they had found because Deacon Ellis sat up late on Sunday nights to put it there. The congregation stood and applauded him for a long time. Marvin wiped his eyes. Afterward he told the young woman that he had been glad to carry the work while it was his to carry, and he was glad now to set it down well. Then he asked her if she could teach him the new app.

wo4-when-it-looks-stale.title: Give It Ten Minutes
wo4-when-it-looks-stale.body: At two minutes past noon, Sister Pamela burst into the media room waving her phone. "It's not there! The service ended five minutes ago and the app still shows last Sunday's message! Is it broken?" Darryl, who ran the media desk, smiled and pulled up a chair for her. "Not broken. Just honest about timing. When the stream ends, the channel takes a few minutes to finish it. And so the whole church isn't all asking the channel at the same time, the app checks it about every ten minutes. Give it a little while." Pamela sat down, not entirely convinced. Darryl handed her a cup of punch from the fellowship hall. At a quarter past twelve he asked her to close the app all the way and open it again. She did. There, at the top of the church page, was that morning's message, already playing, with the date beneath it. Pamela laughed at herself. "So I just have to be patient?" "A few minutes of patience," Darryl said. "Then close and reopen. On a phone, you can pull the page down to refresh it. If it's still wrong after that, then something really is off, and I want to know." Pamela asked how she would tell him. He showed her the Feedback button. "Write what page you're on and what video you expected. It goes straight to the people who build it." Pamela tucked that away. She did not need it that day. But the next week, when a friend panicked over the very same thing at two minutes past noon, Pamela calmly handed her a cup of punch and told her to give it ten minutes.

wo4-when-it-looks-stale.title: The Report That Mattered
wo4-when-it-looks-stale.body: On the Sunday after Thanksgiving, Mrs. Florence Adeyemi opened the church's app at four in the afternoon to rewatch the morning's message for her sister, who had been too sick to come. The top of the church page still showed the previous Sunday's sermon. She waited. She closed the app and reopened it. She pulled down to refresh. An hour later it still had not changed. Florence was not a person who liked to complain. In the old days, with the old website, she would have assumed it was simply how things were and said nothing. But the pastor had told the congregation that if a page looked behind after a refresh, reporting it was a gift, not a bother. So she tapped the Feedback button and wrote, carefully: The church page still shows last Sunday's message at five o'clock. I expected the Thanksgiving weekend service. I have refreshed and reopened twice. On Monday morning the young man who maintained the app read her report first thing. Her words were right there, with the page and the time. He traced it and found that the holiday stream had been saved to the channel in an unusual way, so the app had not recognized it as the newest message. He fixed the problem by noon, and then he made the app handle that case on its own from then on. He wrote back to thank her personally. Florence's sister watched the message that afternoon. Florence thought about how small her report had seemed when she typed it. She had almost not bothered. She realized that knowing the condition of a thing and saying so plainly was its own kind of faithfulness, and that small reports can mend large things.

wo5-ask-for-what-you-want.title: Can It Also Do
wo5-ask-for-what-you-want.body: The choir director, Sister Ophelia, had a wish she had carried for years. She wanted the church's app to show rehearsal times right on the choir page, so the singers would stop texting her every Thursday to ask whether practice was at six or six thirty. With the old website, wishes like that went nowhere. You lived with what the site did. One Thursday, mid-text number nine, she remembered what the pastor had said: if you want something, say it into the app. She tapped the Feedback button, a little embarrassed, and typed exactly what she wanted. Can the choir page show this week's rehearsal time at the top, so the singers can check it themselves? And can I change it from my phone? She hit send and forgot about it. Four days later, a message came back. Her request had been read, written up as a requirement, reviewed, and built. The choir page now had a rehearsal card at the top, with a time she could change from her own phone in two taps. Ophelia stared at it. Then she called her assistant director. "They built it," she said. "I just asked, and they built it." On Thursday not one singer texted her. Not one. She got so excited that she sent in three more wishes that same week. One was built. One was answered with a kind explanation of why it would have to wait, and a date when it would be looked at again. One was merged with someone else's similar idea. Ophelia told the choir that the old way was living with whatever the website did. The new way was the whole house building it together, one voice at a time.

wo5-ask-for-what-you-want.title: The Requests That Vanished
wo5-ask-for-what-you-want.body: Elder Josiah Banks had stopped asking for things. Years earlier, under the church's old website and the outside company that ran it, he had asked for a page listing the names of the church's members who were serving overseas, so the congregation could pray for them by name. He asked once. Then he asked again, six months later. Then a third time. No one ever answered. Not yes, not no, not later. The requests simply vanished, the way requests to faraway companies often do, and after the third silence he quietly concluded that the system was not built to hear people like him. When the church moved to its new app, the pastor told the congregation that anyone could say what they wanted into the app through the Feedback button, and that every request would be answered, either built or given a reason and a date to revisit it. Elder Banks did not believe it. But his granddaughter sat with him one Sunday afternoon and helped him type his old request one more time, word for word as he had written it years before. Nine days later he received an answer. His request had been read by a steward, written up exactly as he had said it, and built. A page now listed those serving overseas, with space for each family to add a prayer request, visible only to the congregation. Elder Banks sat with the tablet in his lap for a long time. Then he opened the page and prayed through every name on it, out loud. He told the pastor the next week that it was not the page that moved him most. It was finally being heard, and his willing heart given a place to bring what it had carried for years.

wi-musk-creator-critique.title: Three Cards at the Barbershop
wi-musk-creator-critique.body: Every Saturday the barbershop on Lincoln Street turned into a courtroom with no judge, and this Saturday the case was the man who owned the new distribution center by the river. A young man named Dorian held up his phone and played a video that said the owner was a crook, a bigot and a polluter, all in four minutes. Heads nodded. Clippers buzzed. Then Miss Loretta, who swept up the hair and had raised half the men in the chairs, pulled three index cards from her apron. On the first she wrote PROVEN. On the second, CLAIMED. On the third, OPINION. "Read it again," she said, "one sentence at a time." The diesel generators the company ran without a permit? Dorian looked it up while his fade was finished. The county record was right there, with dates and a fine. Proven. The jury that found the company liable for how it treated a Black forklift driver? A court verdict. Proven, and Miss Loretta said it plainly, not as a maybe. The video's claim that the owner hated everybody in the neighborhood? No record anywhere, just a voice getting louder. Claimed. The call to never buy anything from him again? Opinion. Then she made Dorian call his cousin, who worked at the center, and hear his side too. By closing time the shop had not settled the owner's soul, and Miss Loretta said that was not their job. But they had written a letter to the county about the generators, signed by eleven men, with the permit number on it. It got an answer in a week.

wi-musk-creator-critique.title: The Plant Beside Cypress Row
wi-musk-creator-critique.body: The plant went up fast beside Cypress Row, a neighborhood founded by freed families after the war and hemmed in ever since by rail yards and smokestacks. Within a year, Ada Fontaine's grandson needed his inhaler twice a night. The neighborhood was angry, and anger is quick to write its own verdicts. At the church meeting someone said the owner should be cursed. Someone else said he must be evil to the bone. Pastor Ellison let them speak, and then he asked Ada to bring what she had. She brought the clinic's records of her grandson's visits, the county's permit with its numbers, and a photograph of the turbines running on nights the permit did not allow. He asked the plant's manager to come and answer, and to everyone's surprise the manager came. He said the turbines were temporary. He said the company had paid for an air monitor. Pastor Ellison heard him out, and then he said what was true. The permit record was documented. The nights the turbines ran without it were documented. The children's visits to the clinic were documented. Those deeds required an account, and repair where harm was done. "What I will not do," he said, looking at the faces in the pews, "is pronounce on this man's soul. That court belongs to Yahweh alone. Our part is to tell the truth about what was done and to stand with the ones who were hurt." It took two years and a hearing. The company paid for filters in forty homes and moved the turbines. Ada's grandson sleeps through the night now, and the church still prays for the manager by name.

wi-beauty-supply-boycott.title: The Distributor's Price List
wi-beauty-supply-boycott.body: Marcus Bell had cut hair on Fairview Avenue for twenty years, and he had always wanted to open a beauty supply store beside his shop. When he finally tried, the big distributors would not return his calls, and the one that did quoted him prices so high he could not compete. He came home steaming. He was ready to tell everyone to stop shopping at the Park family's store on the corner. His daughter Simone, who was sixteen and kept the shop's books, asked him a quiet question. "Daddy, did Mr. Park set those prices?" Marcus opened his mouth and closed it again. He did not know. So Simone did what she did with the books. She wrote down what was documented, the price sheets and the unanswered calls, and what was only assumed. The barrier was real and on paper. Whose hand had built it was a different question. Marcus swallowed his pride and walked down to the corner. Mr. Park listened, frowned, and said the same distributor had treated his own father badly when he started out. He gave Marcus the name of a regional wholesaler who sold on fair terms. Then Marcus called four other Black barbers and stylists in the city and asked them to buy together, so their orders would be big enough to earn a real price. A year later Fairview had two beauty supply stores instead of one. Marcus built his, the Parks kept theirs, and nobody on the avenue had to go to war with a whole people to make it happen.

wi-beauty-supply-boycott.title: The Clerk Who Followed
wi-beauty-supply-boycott.body: Twice that month, a clerk at the corner store had followed Loretta Haynes up and down the aisles, close enough that she could hear him breathing. The second time, she put the basket down and walked out with her face burning. That evening her nephew had the whole neighborhood ready to stop shopping at every store owned by that family's community, all across the city. Loretta sat with it overnight. She knew what it was to be treated as guilty because of your face, and she knew how deep that wound goes. She also knew that what had happened to her had been done by one young man, on two afternoons, in one store. The next morning she went back, and she asked to speak to the owner. She told him exactly what happened, with the days and the times. She did not shout. She did not soften it either. The owner, an older woman named Mrs. Cho, checked the camera footage while Loretta waited. She came back pale. She said what the clerk had done was wrong. She said she would not let him work the floor again, and she apologized, plainly, to Loretta's face. Then she asked if Loretta would help her train the staff, and paid her for it. Loretta's nephew was not satisfied at first. He wanted a bigger fight. But Loretta told him that justice has an address. It goes to the one who did the wrong. It does not burn down a whole street of people who never laid a hand on you.

wi-game-changers-diet.title: Uncle Ray and the Brisket
wi-game-changers-diet.body: Uncle Ray arrived at the family reunion having watched a documentary twice, and he announced, before he had even set down his lawn chair, that meat was poison and every man at the grill was killing himself. The grill went quiet. His niece Danielle, a cardiac nurse, handed him a plate of corn and sat down beside him. "Some of what you saw is true, Uncle Ray," she said, "and I am not going to pretend it isn't." Heart disease, she told him, is the leading killer in the country, and she watches it come through her unit every week. Diets heavy with fried and packaged food do measurable harm. More beans, greens, fruit and whole grains really do help a heart, and in some patients the damage even begins to turn around. She said all that plainly, and Ray nodded hard. "But that test in the film," she went on, "where three men eat one meal and their blood looks cloudy? That is a show, not a study." And calling meat itself evil, she said, goes further than the evidence goes, and further than the Word goes. Yahweh gave food to be received with thanks. Ray chewed on that a while, along with his corn. By the next summer he had cut out the drive-through, filled half his plate with vegetables, and lost twenty-two pounds. And when Danielle's husband sliced the brisket, Uncle Ray bowed his head, gave thanks, and took a modest piece, with a mountain of collards beside it.

wi-game-changers-diet.title: Who Knows
wi-game-changers-diet.body: Walter Greene's favorite words were "who knows." When the doctor said his blood pressure was dangerous, Walter said, "One year eggs are bad, the next year they're good. Who knows?" When his wife put a salad in front of him, he said, "Some study says one thing, another says the opposite." He called it being careful. He said he would not be fooled by fads. And there was some truth in it. He had watched plenty of fads come and go. But the doctor's numbers were not a fad. Heart disease had taken his father at fifty-eight and his older brother James at sixty. That was not a debate. It was two graves in the family plot. One night in the hospital, after a scare that turned out to be a warning and not the end, Walter's grandson sat by the bed and asked, very simply, whether Walter wanted to see him graduate. Walter had no "who knows" for that. He knew. Lying there, he saw that he had used doubt as a hiding place. Some things really were unsettled, and those he could leave narrow. But the plain facts about fried food and soda and a heart like his were not unsettled at all, and pretending they were had been a quiet kind of lie. He went home and let his wife's cooking change him. He still ate the foods Yahweh gave with thanks, a little roast chicken, a piece of fish, but he ate them with vegetables now, and he walked every morning. He was at the graduation, in the third row, standing.

wi-musk-prophetic-lens.title: Can We Hear the Tape?
wi-musk-prophetic-lens.body: Jalen came into his grandmother's kitchen white as flour. A video on his phone said a famous rich man had predicted the end of the world in a recording, and that the recording had been deleted before anyone could save it. The video gave a year. It was two years away. Grandma Odessa wiped her hands and sat down. "Let's hear the recording," she said. Jalen looked. There was no recording. There was a man talking about a recording. There was no copy anywhere, no news report from the time, nothing but people repeating each other. "Baby," she said, "a thing that can never be checked is not a secret revealed. It is a red flag." Then she asked what the rich man had actually said in his own words, in places you could look up. Jalen found some of it, and some of it was strange, and his grandmother did not pretend otherwise. A man's own words are evidence, she said, and you can take them seriously. But she reminded him that the Lord Himself would not set a date, and anybody selling a year was selling something. "Now," she said, standing up, "watching is not the same as worrying." She handed him a trowel. They spent the afternoon putting tomatoes in the ground, and the next Saturday they fixed the loose gutter on the porch. Jalen noticed that the fear had gone out of him somewhere between the third tomato plant and the ladder. Watching, it turned out, looked a lot like building.

wi-musk-prophetic-lens.title: The House Harold Sold
wi-musk-prophetic-lens.body: Harold Simms was a gentle man and a faithful usher, and in the spring he sold his house. He had watched a series of videos that set a date for the end, and the man who made them sounded so sure, and quoted so many things, and named so many powerful people, that Harold believed him. He cashed out his pension early. He gave some away and spent the rest getting ready. He told his grown daughter she would not need college. The date came on a Tuesday. It was a warm, ordinary Tuesday. The buses ran. Children went to school. Harold sat in his small rented room and could not bring himself to come to church that Sunday, or the next. It was the deacon, Mr. Ferris, who finally knocked. He did not say I told you so. He sat on the one chair and let Harold talk. Harold said he had only wanted to be ready. Mr. Ferris said that was a good desire, and watching is a good thing. But a man who sets a date the Lord Himself would not set is not a watchman, he said; he is a voice to be tested. Watching was meant to make a man steady and faithful at his work, not to make him tear his life down. The church helped Harold find a job at the hardware store and a better apartment. It took years to rebuild what the fear had cost. But Harold went back to ushering, and when a young man showed him a video with a date in it, Harold was the one who sat him down.

wi-medical-establishment.title: The White Coat Is Not the Evidence
wi-medical-establishment.body: Bernice had been a nurse for thirty-four years, and her family brought her every health video the way cats bring in birds. This one was from a real doctor with real credentials, and her nephew Curtis said that settled it. Bernice poured two cups of coffee and pulled out a legal pad. "A white coat is not evidence," she said, "and evidence does not need a white coat. We weigh each claim by itself." The doctor said drug makers are shielded from ordinary lawsuits over certain injuries. Bernice looked it up with him. There was a real federal law, and a real compensation fund. True, and she said so. The doctor said most medical students get very little training in nutrition. Bernice laughed. "I could have told you that. True."
