Her teacher smiled and said, "Let's check." So Ava went to the library with her great-grandma, Nana Bee. Nana Bee was ninety-two. The librarian found an old book of photos. On one page was a picture of a city street in 1900. It was full of electric taxis! Ava's mouth fell open. The book said that back then, about one in three cars on the road was electric. People liked them because they were quiet and clean. They did not need a hand crank to start. Ava asked why they went away. The book explained. Gas got cheap. Roads got longer. Batteries could not go very far. So most people switched to gas cars. Nana Bee laughed softly. "My mother rode in an electric taxi when she was a girl," she said. Ava could hardly believe it. She went back to class and told the real story. Electric cars were not new at all. They had come early, and then come back. The teacher said that is what history is for.

car5-the-electric-car-came-early.title: The Son Who Laughed at His Father
car5-the-electric-car-came-early.body: When Henry was young, he used to laugh at his father. His father had kept an old wood stove in the kitchen for years. "Why didn't you just get a good stove?" Henry would ask. His father would only shrug and say, "It was what we had." Henry thought his father was old-fashioned. He thought he did not know any better. Many years later, after his father had died, Henry found a box of old papers. In it were letters and bills from the year Henry was born. Henry read them slowly. There was no gas line to their road then. The power often went out in winter. A new stove cost more than his father earned in three months. And the wood stove had kept baby Henry warm through a terrible storm. The whole town had lost power for a week. Henry put the letters down. His eyes filled with tears. His father had not been foolish at all. He had made a wise choice with what he had. Henry had judged him by what people have now. Henry kept that box. He shows his own children the letters. He tells them to always ask what people knew and had back then.

car6-who-is-driving.title: Level Two, Dad
car6-who-is-driving.body: Dad got a new car. It could keep itself in the lane and slow down by itself. On the first drive, Dad took his hands off the wheel. "Look, kids! It drives itself!" Mia, who was nine, did not like that. She grabbed the owner's book from the glove box. She found a page with a chart. The chart had levels, from zero to five. Level five meant a car that could drive anywhere all by itself. Mia found their car. It was level two. Under level two, the book said, The driver must drive and watch the road at all times. Mia read it out loud. "Dad, it's level two. That means you are still the driver." Dad put his hands back on the wheel. "Well," he said, "I guess I believed the ad and not the book." Mom laughed. Then a car ahead stopped fast. The new car did beep. But Dad was the one who pressed the brake, right on time. Everyone was safe. Dad looked at Mia in the mirror. "Thanks, captain," he said. Mia said the most important level was the one where you know who is in charge.

car6-who-is-driving.title: Who Answers for the Shuttle?
car6-who-is-driving.body: The town of Brookfield got a little bus with no driver. It ran around the park on a fixed route. Mr. Grant owned the company that ran it. He was very proud. One morning the shuttle did not see a bike rider in the rain. It bumped her bike and she fell. She broke her arm. Everyone in town asked the same question. Who was responsible? There was no driver to blame. Some people blamed the computer. Some blamed the rain. Mr. Grant's lawyer said nobody was really at fault. Mr. Grant thought about it all night. He remembered an old rule his grandfather taught him. If you own something that can hurt people, and you know it, you must answer for it. Mr. Grant knew the shuttle had trouble in the rain. His workers had warned him. He had kept it running anyway. The next day he went to see the bike rider. Her name was Mrs. Lopez. He told her the truth. He said it was his fault. He paid her doctor bills and her lost work. And he stopped the shuttle on rainy days until it was fixed. Mrs. Lopez forgave him. She said she was glad someone answered.

econ1-soul-first.title: The Raise and the Question
econ1-soul-first.body: The day Terrence got his first big raise, he drove straight to his grandmother's house to tell her. He had it all planned out. A newer car, a bigger apartment, maybe a watch. He talked for ten minutes without stopping. Grandma Inez listened, smiling, shelling peas into a bowl. When he finally ran out of breath, she asked him one question. "And how is your soul, baby?" Terrence laughed. Then he stopped laughing, because she was not joking. He thought about it. He had not been to church in two months. He had been short with his little brother. He had been working so hard he had not slept well since spring. "Not as good as my paycheck," he admitted. Grandma Inez nodded. She told him that money was a wonderful servant and a cruel boss, and that a man whose wallet grows faster than his soul is heading somewhere he does not want to go. Then she said something else. She had heard him repeating a statistic last month at the cookout, one that made their community sound better than the numbers showed. She had looked it up. It was not true. "Don't flatter yourself with things that aren't so," she said, "and don't hide from the hard things that are. The truth is what does a people good, even when it stings." Terrence went home and did not buy the watch. He went back to church that Sunday. He started a savings account, and he called his little brother. A year later he bought the car, paid in cash, and drove Grandma Inez to service in it.

econ1-soul-first.title: The Richest Man at Greater Zion
econ1-soul-first.body: Brother Calvin Monroe was the richest man at Greater Zion Baptist, and for twenty years he gave the most. His name was on the fellowship hall. He sat on every board. Everyone said Yahweh had blessed him, and Calvin believed it, and slowly he came to believe something else too. He came to believe that his money proved his standing with the Lord, and that the poorer members, who gave less, must somehow be less faithful. He never said it out loud. But he voted that way on the boards, and he spoke that way at the meetings, and the young people felt it. Then his business failed. It failed all at once, through a partner's fraud he had not seen coming. In eighteen months Calvin lost the business, the big house and most of his savings. He sat in the back pew for the first time in two decades, ashamed to be seen. It was old Sister Odell, who cleaned offices for a living, who sat down beside him. She did not mention the money. She asked him how he was doing, and she meant his heart. Calvin found he could not answer. He realized he had not asked himself that question in twenty years. His soul had been starving the whole time his bank account was full. Over the next year, Sister Odell and a few others walked with him. He learned to pray again, and to tell the truth about what he had believed. He rebuilt slowly. When he finally prospered again, it was a different kind of prospering, and he never again mistook a full wallet for a healthy soul.

econ2-ownership-vs-consumption.title: Two Sisters, Two Thousand Dollars
econ2-ownership-vs-consumption.body: When their grandfather passed, Keisha and Tamara each inherited two thousand dollars. Keisha was nineteen and had been wanting new things for a long time. Within a month she had a new phone, a closet full of clothes and a weekend trip with her friends. It was fun. By summer it was all used up, the clothes out of style and the trip a few photos. Tamara thought for a long time. Then she spent eleven hundred dollars on a commercial pressure washer and a used trailer, and five hundred more on flyers and a business license. She kept four hundred in the bank. Keisha laughed at her. Who spends their inheritance on a machine that sprays water? But by July, Tamara was washing driveways, decks and storefronts six days a week. She charged fair prices and did careful work, and people told their neighbors. By the end of the year she had earned nine thousand dollars, and she hired a boy from church to help her. The next spring she bought a second washer. Keisha watched all this with growing interest and a little embarrassment. One evening she asked her sister how she had known what to do. Tamara said she had been thinking about the servants in the story Jesus told, the ones who put their master's money to work instead of burying it. "Grandpa worked his whole life for that money," she said. "I wanted it to keep working." Keisha nodded slowly. Two years later the sisters ran the business together, and they had already started saving for their own children's inheritance.

econ2-ownership-vs-consumption.title: The Coffee Can
econ2-ownership-vs-consumption.body: Mr. Ezekiel Barnes did not trust banks. He had good reasons. When he was a young man, a bank had refused him a loan because of where he lived, and a lender had cheated his father out of his house. So for forty years Ezekiel saved every dollar he could in a coffee can buried under the shed. He worked hard. He spent almost nothing. He was proud of that can. When he died, his grandson Isaiah dug it up. Inside was eighteen thousand dollars in old bills, carefully wrapped. It was a lot of saving. But Isaiah, who worked at a credit union, did the math that night with a heavy heart. If his grandfather had put that same money into a home, or a small business, or even a simple fund that grew, it would have been worth many times more. Prices had climbed for forty years, and every year the money in the can had quietly bought less and less. His grandfather had been faithful and fearful at the same time. The fear had been earned. But it had kept the money in the ground. Isaiah thought about the servant in the parable who buried his talent because he was afraid. He did not judge his grandfather harshly. He knew what had been done to him. But he decided the fear would stop with him. He took the eighteen thousand and used it as the down payment on a small duplex. He lived in one side and rented the other. Twenty years later, that duplex had paid for itself, and Isaiah's own children knew exactly whose coffee can had started it all.

econ3-circulation.title: The Twenty with the Ribbon
econ3-circulation.body: Deacon Harold Mims wanted to show the youth group what circulation meant, so he took a twenty-dollar bill, tied a thin red ribbon around one corner, and spent it at Miss Bertha's soul food café on Monroe Street. He asked Miss Bertha to spend it at another business owned by someone in the neighborhood and to text him where it went. She bought produce from Mr. Akins's corner market. Mr. Akins paid the young man who fixed his cooler. The young man got a haircut at Lewis's barbershop. Lewis bought a cake from a church member who baked from home. The baker paid her daughter's piano teacher. By the end of the month that one twenty had met six needs on four blocks before it finally left the neighborhood at a gas station. The youth group loved it. Then one of the boys, Jerome, raised his hand and said something he had heard on a podcast, that a dollar only stays in the Black community for six hours. Deacon Mims smiled. He had looked that number up. Nobody had ever measured it, and there was no data that could. "We don't need a number we can't prove," he said. Then he pulled out a page from the Federal Reserve. The typical white family held about six times the wealth of the typical Black family, a gap of nearly a quarter of a million dollars. "That one is real," he said, "and it's worse than the myth." Jerome was quiet. Then he asked if the youth group could do the ribbon again, with five bills this time.

econ3-circulation.title: Friday Afternoon on Carver Avenue
econ3-circulation.body: On Carver Avenue, payday was Friday, and by Friday evening the money was gone. Not spent badly, just gone. Rent went to a landlord who lived two counties away. Groceries went to a chain store whose owners had never seen the street. Checks were cashed at a storefront that took a cut of every one. Even the corner store was owned by a man who drove in each morning and drove out each night. Mrs. Odessa Lane had lived on Carver for fifty-one years, and she had watched it happen slowly. When she was a girl, there had been a Black-owned grocery, a pharmacy, a bank and two funeral homes on the avenue. Some had been squeezed out by lenders who would not lend there. Some had been bought up. Now the street worked hard every week and kept almost nothing. It was not lack of effort. Everyone she knew worked. It was that every dollar left on Friday and none came back. Mrs. Lane read in her Bible how the Lord taught His people to provide for the poor among them, and she thought the street had forgotten how to provide for itself. So at seventy-three, she started small. She talked her church into opening a little credit union in the basement. She asked her neighbors to bank there, even with ten dollars. She talked the pastor into buying the empty pharmacy building. It took eight years. But now on Friday, some of the money stays. A young pharmacist from the church runs the old store. And the credit union has made its first two home loans on Carver Avenue in sixty years.

econ4-group-economics.title: The Susu on Maple Street
econ4-group-economics.body: Ten women from Maple Street Church sat around Sister Abena's kitchen table on the first Sunday of every month, and each one brought two hundred dollars in an envelope. Abena had learned it from her mother in Ghana. They called it a susu. Each month, one woman took home the whole pot, two thousand dollars, and the next month it went to the next woman, until all ten had received it once. Then they started again. Nobody paid interest. Nobody needed a bank's approval. They only needed to trust each other, and they did. At first the younger women thought it was old-fashioned. Then Monique's car died in March, and her turn came early because the others agreed to swap. She bought a reliable used car with cash, and kept her job. In June, Lorraine used her pot to put a deposit on a commercial kitchen and started a catering business. In September, Sister Abena's turn paid for her grandson's first semester of trade school. By the end of the year, the circle had moved twenty thousand dollars through ten households, and not one dollar had gone to a lender. Monique laughed and said she had never been so rich with so little. Abena said that was the whole idea. One woman alone, she said, could save two hundred dollars a month and wait a year. Ten women together could put two thousand in someone's hands right now, when she needed it. The next year the circle had grown to twenty, and they split into two tables. Lorraine catered the celebration.

econ4-group-economics.title: The Burial Society
econ4-group-economics.body: In 1911, when the insurance companies in town would not write a policy for a Black family, eleven men from Bethel Church met in a blacksmith's shop and started the Bethel Benevolent Society. Each man paid ten cents a week. When a member died, the society paid for a decent burial and gave the widow enough to live on for three months. It was not much money. But it was more than anyone else would give them. Old Mr. Samuel Hayes was the last living member who remembered those early days, and on his ninety-fifth birthday his great-granddaughter Naomi asked him to tell her about it. He told her how hard it was. Ten cents was a lot in a week when a man made two dollars. Some weeks men went without lunch to pay their share. When the influenza came through in 1918, the society buried fourteen members in two months, and the treasury nearly ran dry. The men met in the blacksmith's shop and prayed, and then they doubled their dues, and their wives took in extra washing to make it. They did not quit. Every widow was paid. By the 1940s the society had grown so large that it became a real insurance company, owned by the people it served, and it lent money to build the first Black-owned homes on the east side. Naomi asked him how they did it. Mr. Hayes said the people simply decided to work together, and no one could break eleven men holding the same rope. Naomi works at a community bank now. She keeps the society's first ledger in a glass frame on her office wall.

econ5-the-real-barriers.title: The Clause in the Deed
econ5-the-real-barriers.body: When Andre and Simone Baptiste bought their first house, a little brick bungalow on Linden Street, they were so happy they read every page of the closing papers out loud to each other. On page eleven of the old deed, copied forward from 1926, Simone stopped reading. The words said that no part of the property should ever be sold to or occupied by any person of African descent. She read it again. Andre took the paper from her hand and read it himself. They were sitting in a house that, by those words, they were never supposed to own. Their lawyer explained that the clause had been made unenforceable by the Supreme Court in 1948 and could not stop them. It was dead ink. But it was real ink. Somebody had written it, a court had once enforced it, and for twenty-two years it had kept families like theirs off Linden Street, out of the very houses that built most American families' wealth. Simone went to the county records office and found that more than half the deeds in their neighborhood had the same clause. She also found the old federal map that had marked the neighborhood across the tracks, where her grandparents lived, as too risky for any loan. That was not an accusation. It was paper. Andre and Simone did two things. They filed to have the clause formally struck from their deed, which the state now allowed. And they framed a copy of the original page and hung it in the hallway. When their children ask about it, Andre tells them plainly what it says, and then tells them whose house it is now.

econ5-the-real-barriers.title: The Veteran and the Red Line
econ5-the-real-barriers.body: Corporal James Whitaker came home from the war in 1946 with a medal, a bad leg and a promise. The government had promised every returning soldier help buying a home. He saved his pay for two years, found a little house near the factory where he worked, and went to the bank with his papers. The loan officer did not look at his medal or his papers for long. He looked at a map on the wall, where the neighborhood James had chosen was shaded red. The bank did not lend there, the man said. And the neighborhoods that were not shaded red did not sell to men like James. It was not personal, the man said. It was policy. James walked out into the sunshine and stood on the steps for a long time. The white soldiers he had served beside were buying houses that year with the same promise. Over the next thirty years those houses would quietly double and triple in value, and they would be passed down to children and grandchildren. James rented his whole life. He worked hard. He never missed a payment on anything. When he died, he left his family his medal and some furniture. Fifty years later his granddaughter, a housing attorney named Dana, found that same bank's map in a university archive, with the same red shading and the same date. She brought a copy to a hearing on lending fairness and laid it on the table. She told them about her grandfather's medal. She said this was not a story about effort. It was a story about a line someone drew, and she was there to speak for those who were never allowed to speak for themselves.

econ6-accountability-and-judgment.title: The Branch Manager's Refund
econ6-accountability-and-judgment.body: Kevin Adler had managed the Elm Street bank branch for six years, and he was proud of its numbers. Then the main office ran an audit, and Kevin was handed a report that made him sick. For years before he arrived, and for two years after, the branch had charged higher fees and higher rates to customers from three particular zip codes on the south side. It was buried in the pricing system, and no one at the branch had questioned it. Kevin had approved the pricing every quarter without looking. He could have blamed the system, or the managers before him, or the main office. Many people around him did exactly that. But Kevin went home and could not stop thinking about one thing. He would not stand before the Lord someday as part of a system. He would stand there as himself, and give his own account. So he went back the next morning and asked the main office for the list of every affected customer. He pushed until they agreed to refund every dollar, with interest. When the letters went out, he signed each one himself. One elderly woman, Mrs. Esther Polk, came into the branch with her letter in her hand and asked to see the manager. Kevin was nervous. She looked at him a long while and then said she had suspected for years that she was being overcharged, and that she had always told the Lord about it. "He saw it," she said. "And now you've seen it too." Kevin told her he was sorry, and that it would not happen again on his watch. It did not.

econ6-accountability-and-judgment.title: The Woman Who Was Seen
econ6-accountability-and-judgment.body: In 1962, Mrs. Clara Wynn cleaned houses for a wealthy family across town. For three years Mr. Harlan Price paid her less than he had promised, and when she asked about it, he said she was lucky to have work at all. She had four children and no one to complain to. No court would have heard her. She went home on those nights and sat in her kitchen, and she told the Lord. She told Him the exact amount, every week. She did not know if He was keeping count, but she was. She believed He saw her, and she held onto that. Sixty years later, a man in his seventies knocked on the door of the small house where Clara's daughter, Loretta, now lived. His name was Thomas Price. He was Mr. Harlan's son. He had been going through his late father's papers and found a notebook in which his father had written down every week he had shorted Mrs. Wynn, and how much. Thomas had added it up. Then he had added what it would be worth today, and then more. He held out a check with his hands shaking. He said he could not undo it. He said he could only confess it and repay it. Loretta sat down on the porch steps and wept. Her mother had died believing someone was keeping count. She had been right. Yahweh had seen every week, and He had covered Clara's children all those years in ways the money never could. Loretta took the check. Then she invited Thomas inside for coffee, and they sat at her mother's old kitchen table and talked until dark.

econ7-build-institutions.title: Twelve Families and a Credit Union
econ7-build-institutions.body: It started with twelve families and a folding table in the back of Mount Calvary Church. Every family put in five hundred dollars. Brother Clarence Hughes, a retired accountant, filed the paperwork. They called it the Calvary Community Credit Union, and on opening day it had six thousand dollars and one account book. People laughed a little. What could six thousand dollars do? The first loan was nine hundred dollars to a young mother named Tasha, so she could fix her car and keep her job. She paid it back early. The second was to a man who needed tools to start a lawn business. Then a woman who wanted to open a daycare. Every loan was small, and every borrower was known, and almost every one was repaid. The credit union paid fair interest to its savers and charged fair interest to its borrowers, and the money stayed in the neighborhood. Ten years later it had four million dollars, two branches and a staff of nine. Tasha was its loan officer. The daycare had grown to three locations. Brother Clarence was ninety by then. At the anniversary dinner, someone asked him what he was proudest of. He said it was not the four million dollars. It was that the credit union would still be there long after he was gone, and long after everyone in the room was gone. His grandchildren would bank there, and their grandchildren too. "A paycheck ends when you stop working," he said. "This keeps working when we're all in the ground." Then he sat down, and the whole room stood up.

econ7-build-institutions.title: What Was Never Repaid
econ7-build-institutions.body: Delores Freeman's great-grandfather had owned a dry goods store in a thriving Black business district in a southern city, the kind of place where a dollar could pass through a dozen hands and every one of them belonged to a neighbor. In two terrible days, a mob burned the whole district. The store was gone. The family's savings were gone. A commission years later said the survivors should be repaid. No one ever paid them. Delores grew up hearing the story at every Thanksgiving, told quietly, with a photograph of the store passed hand to hand. For a long time it only made her angry. She was angry at the mob, at the city, at the decades of silence. The anger was right. What happened was a real, documented wrong, and she never pretended otherwise. But at forty-five, sitting with that photograph after her mother's funeral, she felt something else rise up underneath the anger. Her great-grandfather had built that store. Nobody had handed it to him. He had built it, and so had his neighbors, a whole economy owned by the people it served, and it had worked. Delores was a pharmacist. She talked to six other professionals from her church, a dentist, two nurses, an electrician, a lawyer and a teacher, and they pooled their savings and bought a building. They opened a pharmacy, a dental clinic and a small business center under one roof, owned together by the seven of them and their families. Her pastor told her not to be afraid and to see the work through to the end. On the wall in the entry hangs the photograph of the dry goods store.

econ8-test-build-multiply.title: The Waiting List Bakery
econ8-test-build-multiply.body: For years Renée Abara dreamed of opening a bakery, and for years her friends told her to just do it. Her pound cakes were famous at church. But a storefront would cost her almost all her savings, and Renée had watched too many people sign leases on dreams and lose everything. So she did something slower. She made a simple sign-up sheet. Anyone who wanted a cake each month could put down their name and their order. She told people the truth. She was testing whether there was enough demand to open a shop, and the list was the test. She did not pretend there were only a few spots left. She did not invent a countdown. If nobody signed, she would know. Forty people signed the first week. Then seventy. By the end of two months there were a hundred and thirty names, and twelve of them were businesses that wanted cakes for their offices. Renée baked in a rented church kitchen on weekends and delivered every order herself, on time, the way she said she would. People told their friends. Her name got around, and it was a good name, because she kept her word. Only then did she look for a shop. She found a small one, counted every cost twice, and signed a lease she could pay even if half the list disappeared. It did not disappear. It grew. A year after opening she trained two young women from her church to run a second oven. Renée still keeps that first sign-up sheet in a frame by the register. She says it was the cheapest, smartest thing she ever built.

econ8-test-build-multiply.title: The Restaurant Nobody Asked For
econ8-test-build-multiply.body: Marcus Fields had a dream, and he loved it so much he never tested it. He wanted to open an upscale restaurant in his old neighborhood, with white tablecloths and a menu that would make people proud. He did not ask anyone if they would eat there. He did not count what it would really cost. He took out a second mortgage, emptied his retirement account and borrowed from his brother. He spent eight months and every dollar building a beautiful dining room. On opening night his family came, and a few friends. The next night there were nine customers. Within a month most nights there were three or four. The neighborhood was proud of him, but most families there could not afford forty-dollar plates, and the people who could did not drive across town to eat. Marcus had built the house before he had planted the field. In eleven months the restaurant closed. Marcus owed more than he would earn in five years. He did not leave his house for weeks. It was his pastor who finally sat with him. He did not shame him. He told him Jesus Himself had warned about the man who starts a tower and cannot finish it, not to mock that man, but so others would count first. Marcus was that man now, the pastor said gently, which meant Marcus could teach others what it cost. It took him seven years to pay back his brother. Then he started over, small this time. He sold plates from a food truck and kept a list of every customer who asked for more. When he finally opened a little lunch counter, it was full on the first day.

pv-price.title: The Choir Director's Seating Chart
pv-price.body: Everyone at First Community Church loved Brother Ellis Grant. He had directed the choir for twenty-two years, and when he lifted his hands the whole sanctuary seemed to lift with him. So when he asked to speak at the annual meeting, people expected a report on robes and hymnals. Instead he unrolled an old seating chart he had found in the church basement. It was from the year the church was founded, and it showed the balcony marked off for Black members only. Then he unrolled a second chart. It was this year's. Nobody had drawn any lines on it. But when he marked where people actually sat, the old pattern was still there, almost exactly. The Black families sat on one side, the white families on the other, the newcomers from Mexico in the back. Nobody had planned it. Everybody had done it. The room went very quiet. A few people were angry. One board member said Brother Grant had no business stirring things up, and two families left that spring. Brother Grant knew they might. He said Yahweh does not rank His children by color, and a church that keeps the old lines without drawing them is still keeping them. Then he did a simple thing. He asked the choir, which was the only truly mixed group in the building, to sit scattered throughout the congregation on Sunday mornings instead of up front together. Every week the choir members sat beside someone new and learned their name. It took a year. But the next time someone marked the seating chart, there were no sides left to mark.

pv-price.title: The Founding Minutes
pv-price.body: Reverend Thaddeus Moore had pastored Calvary Church for thirty years and built it into one of the largest congregations in the state. He had a radio program, a book, and friends in every important pulpit in the country. He had, as his wife once said, everything to lose. In his thirty-first year, while preparing the church's anniversary history, he read the original minutes from 1859. They showed that the founding members had voted, after a sermon, to bless the holding of human beings as property, and that several of them had been slaveholders. The minutes even recorded the Scripture passages twisted to support it. Reverend Moore read them three times. Then he did what almost no one in his position would do. On anniversary Sunday, in front of five thousand people and the radio audience, he read the minutes aloud. He said plainly that the church of Jesus Christ had sided with evil instead of with the Word, and that slavery could never have stood as long as it did if the churches of the land had refused it. Yahweh, he said, favors no race over another. A church that blessed the chains had betrayed its own Lord. The radio station canceled his program within the month. Two other pastors stopped returning his calls. Some members left. Reverend Moore did not take back a word. He spent the next ten years helping his congregation make repair, funding scholarships and rebuilding a cemetery for the enslaved that the church had let fall into ruin. When he died, the descendants of those buried there carried his casket.

pv-darby.title: Miss Hattie Said It First
pv-darby.body: For thirty years, Miss Hattie Blue taught history at Lincoln High in her small Kentucky town, and for thirty years she taught the parts the textbook left out. She taught her students about the Black families who had founded half the town's churches and businesses. She taught them about the land that had been taken and the names that had been erased. She brought old deeds and photographs to class. Some parents complained. The school board told her more than once to stick to the book. Folks in town said she was bitter, that she dwelt on the past, that she ought to let it go. She kept teaching. When she retired, there was a small cake in the teacher's lounge, and that was all. Ten years later, a young historian from a big university came to town to write a book about its forgotten history. She was celebrated. The newspaper ran her picture. The town council gave her an award and held a reception in the library. At the reception, a gray-haired man stood up and asked to say something. He was the mayor now, but he had been in Miss Hattie's class forty years before. He said everything the young historian had found, Miss Hattie had taught him at sixteen. He said the town had honored the stranger and ignored the prophet in its own backyard. The room went quiet. The young historian stood up too, and said she had read Miss Hattie's old notes in the library archive, and that her whole book was built on them. That spring, the town renamed the library for Miss Hattie Blue. She was ninety-one. She cut the ribbon herself.

pv-darby.title: The Man Who Read the Record Aloud
pv-darby.body: Every year the town of Millbrook held a founders' celebration, and every year the mayor gave the same speech about the brave pioneers who built the town from nothing. One year a quiet man named Stephen Hollis asked for five minutes at the town meeting beforehand. He was a deacon and a retired postal worker, and nobody expected much. He stood up with a stack of copies he had made at the county archive. He read them aloud, one by one. He read the deed that showed the land had been taken from Black farmers by a forged lien. He read the minutes of the council that had voted to keep Black children out of the town school for fifty years. He read the newspaper story praising the men who had driven a Black pastor out of town in 1919, and he read the names. Some of those names belonged to families sitting in the room. He did not shout. He did not insult anyone. He simply read their own history back to them, and asked them to repent and repair it. The room turned on him. People shouted him down before he finished. The mayor had him escorted out. In the weeks that followed, someone painted words on his garage. His church asked him to step down as deacon to keep the peace. Stephen did not stop. He gave his copies to the library and kept speaking wherever anyone would let him. He died a few years later, mostly forgotten. But a young woman who had been in the room that night never forgot. Twenty years later, as mayor, she read his copies aloud at the founders' celebration. And this time the room listened.

pv-diop.title: Count the Rings
pv-diop.body: Every child in Oak Hollow knew the story of the great oak in the town square. The founders had planted it, everyone said, on the day the town began in 1870. There was even a plaque. Nobody had ever questioned it. Then a ninth grader named Amara Diallo, who loved science more than anything, noticed something. When a storm took down one of the oak's huge branches, she asked the town if she could count the rings on the cut end. The town said sure, though a few people rolled their eyes. Amara borrowed a magnifying glass from her teacher, sanded the cut smooth, and counted every ring, twice. Then she used the branch's position and a formula from a forestry book to estimate the age of the whole tree. Her answer was about three hundred years. The oak had been standing more than a century before the founders ever arrived. Some people did not believe her. One man said a girl with a magnifying glass could not overturn a plaque. Amara did not argue. She invited the county forester to check her work, and he did, and he got almost exactly her number. She also wrote down plainly which parts were measured and which were estimated, so no one could say she had overclaimed. The town changed the plaque. It now says the oak was already old when the town was young, and that it was there first. Amara's teacher hung a copy of her ring count in the science room. Under it she wrote that the truth does not mind being tested. It is the assumption that minds.

pv-diop.title: The Scientist Who Stood Almost Alone
pv-diop.body: Dr. Mariama Sow was trained as a chemist in a great university overseas, and she came home to build the first dating laboratory her country had ever had. She built it with borrowed equipment and her own hands. She had one question she wanted to answer with evidence instead of assumption. For a century, scholars from distant countries had told her people that the ancient kingdom whose ruins stood in the river valley could not have been built by their own ancestors. It must have been built by outsiders, they said. No one had ever tested it. They had simply assumed it. So Dr. Sow tested it. She dated the materials. She measured the remains. She mapped the language and customs that connected the old kingdom to the villages still living along the river. Year after year, her findings pointed the same direction. The kingdom had been built by the people who still lived there. When she presented her work at an international conference, she and one colleague stood almost entirely alone. The room was polite and closed. Some of her conclusions, she freely admitted, were still uncertain and needed more work, and she said so plainly. But the central question had been answered by evidence, and the room did not want to hear it. She went home and kept working. She trained students. She published everything. She died before the field fully listened. But her students carried on, and slowly the textbooks began to change. What had been hidden under a century of assumption came, at last, to light, as hidden things do.

pv-obenga.title: Grandma's Words
pv-obenga.body: Kwame's grandmother had a word for everything, and most of the words were not English. When she was pleased she said one word. When she wanted the children to come eat she said another. She called the river and the moon and a newborn baby by names her own grandmother had used. Kwame had always thought they were just Grandma's special words. Then in college, Kwame took a class on African languages. One afternoon the professor put a list on the board, words from a village language spoken more than three thousand miles from where Kwame's family had lived for generations in South Carolina. Kwame sat up straight. Six of the words on the board were Grandma's words. Not almost the same. The same, sound for sound, meaning for meaning. He raised his hand, his voice shaking a little, and told the class. The professor smiled. She said that was what languages did. A people could be carried across an ocean. Their names could be changed on paper. Their history could be left out of every book. But the words they used for supper and babies and rivers often survived, passed from mouth to ear across ten generations, testifying to where they came from. Nobody could chisel that away. Kwame called his grandmother that night and told her. She laughed and laughed. Then she said she had always known where they came from. She just had not known the rest of the world could see it too. Kwame went on to study languages. His first paper was a list of Grandma's words, each one traced home.

pv-obenga.title: The Names on the Map
pv-obenga.body: When the conquerors came to the valley of Asumé, they renamed everything. The river became the Victoria. The mountain became Mount Prospect. The old market town became Port Albert. They printed the new names on every map, carved them on every stone, and taught them in every school. Children were punished for using the old names. The old records were burned. Within two generations, the official history said the valley had been an empty wilderness before the conquerors arrived, and that no one had named it until they did. But the people of the valley kept singing. At harvest, at weddings, at funerals, the old women sang the old songs, and in the songs the river was still called Asumé, and the mountain still had its old name, and the market town was still called by the name that meant meeting place of the clans. The songs were full of names that were not on any map. A young scholar named Ngozi grew up hearing those songs. When she was grown, she spent years writing them down, comparing them village to village, tracing how the names and their meanings had been carried, unchanged, for centuries. The conquerors had controlled the maps and the stones and the schools. But they had never controlled what grandmothers sang to babies. Ngozi published her findings, and the government argued with her, and she kept publishing. The song names held. They held because they were true and had been carried by thousands of mouths. Forty years later, the river's old name was printed on the maps again. Ngozi was there when they unveiled the new sign. The old women sang.

pv-williams.title: The Fence and the Flood
pv-williams.body: The Turner brothers, Clyde and Roy, had farmed side by side for thirty years, and for twenty-nine of those years they had not spoken. It started over a fence line, two feet of ground that each was sure belonged to him. Clyde built the fence one way. Roy tore it down and built it another. Their wives stopped speaking. Their children grew up on opposite sides of the property and were told not to play together. The whole county knew about the Turner feud. Then one spring the creek began to rise. The old levee that protected both farms had needed work for years, but each brother had refused to fix the part that touched the other's land. Now the water was coming, and it did not care where the fence was. On the second night of rain, Roy's son, who was seventeen, walked across the field in the dark and knocked on Clyde's door. He said the levee would break by morning unless both families worked together. Clyde stood in the doorway a long time. Then he got his boots. All night, both families filled sandbags side by side in the rain, the brothers working shoulder to shoulder without saying a word. By dawn the levee held. Both farms were saved. Roy and Clyde stood on the levee in the gray light, soaked and exhausted, looking at the water. Finally Clyde said that the flood would have taken both of them while they argued about two feet of ground. Roy nodded. That summer the fence came down for good, and the two families rebuilt the levee together, stronger than before.

pv-williams.title: The Elder's Mirror
pv-williams.body: The old men of the village tell this story at the beginning of every gathering. Long ago there were seven clans in the valley, and together they were strong. They traded with each other and married each other and defended each other, and no raiders dared to come. But over the years the clans began to quarrel. One clan said another was cheating at the market. One said another had insulted its elders. Small grudges grew into old feuds. The clans stopped trading. They stopped marrying across lines. They stopped coming to each other's aid. When raiders came at last, they did not have to fight seven clans. They fought one at a time, and the others watched and did nothing, each one glad it was not its turn. Within a generation the valley was lost. The oldest elder, a woman named Nana Akosua, survived and gathered the children of every clan around her. She did not only speak of the raiders, though she named them and what they had done. She held up a polished bronze mirror and turned it toward the children. She told them the raiders were real and their cruelty was real. But the raiders had only been able to do what the clans' division had already made possible. A divided people, she said, has already opened its own gate, and the hardest enemy to see is the one in the mirror. Then she taught the children everything the clans had forgotten, the old trade routes, the old marriage ties, the old promises. A people who lost their knowledge, she said, can be rebuilt by recovering it. The children of those children rebuilt the valley.

pv-inventions.title: The Dated Notebook
pv-inventions.body: For the science fair, Aaliyah had an idea. She would build a small water filter for camping out of sand, charcoal and an old soda bottle, and make it cheap enough for any family. She worked on it for weeks, and she wrote everything down in a notebook her grandfather gave her, with the date at the top of every page. She sketched each version. She wrote down what worked and what did not. One day she showed her design to a classmate named Brett, who said it was cool. Two weeks later, at the fair, Brett had a water filter of his own. It was almost exactly like hers. When the judges came to his table, he explained it as if he had thought of it all himself. When they came to hers, they said it looked a lot like Brett's. Aaliyah felt sick. She wanted to cry. Instead she thought about her grandfather, who always said the record tells the truth if you keep it. She opened her notebook and showed the judges her sketches, one after another, each with its date, going back six weeks. She showed the page where she first wrote down the idea. The judges looked at Brett's papers. His earliest page was dated four days after he had seen her notebook. They asked him about it, and he went red and admitted it. Aaliyah won first place. Brett apologized to her afterward, and she forgave him. Her grandfather framed the first page of the notebook. He said the truth has a way of coming out, and it helps when somebody writes the date at the top.

pv-inventions.title: The Plow in the Drawing
pv-inventions.body: In 1851 on a plantation in the low country, an enslaved blacksmith named Josiah designed a new kind of plow. It turned the heavy, wet soil of the river fields in half the time and with half the strength. He built the first one by hand at his forge, working at night after the day's labor. The plow worked so well that planters from three counties came to see it. The man who claimed to own Josiah, a planter named Caldwell, sent the design to the patent office under his own name. The law of that day said an enslaved man could not hold a patent, and so the law helped Caldwell take it. Caldwell sold the rights and grew rich. Josiah received nothing, not even his name on the paper. He died in 1863, a few months before freedom reached the plantation. But before he died, he gave his grandson a folded drawing of the plow, in his own hand, with his own mark at the bottom. The family kept it for a hundred and forty years. In 2003 Josiah's great-great-granddaughter, a lawyer named Renee, took the drawing to a historian, who matched it line for line to the patent drawing filed under Caldwell's name. Same curves, same measurements, same small mistake in one corner that Josiah had made and Caldwell's clerk had copied. Renee presented it to the state historical society, and they changed the record. The plow now carries Josiah's name. Renee said the robbery had been legal, but it had never been hidden from Yahweh. He does not forget the ones who are robbed, and in His time, the record comes home.

lil1-a-is-for-adam-who-named-the-animals.title: Lily Names the Garden Friends
lil1-a-is-for-adam-who-named-the-animals.body: Lily went out to the garden with Grandpa. She had a new notebook and a fat red crayon. "Today we are namers," Grandpa said. "Just like Adam." A brown hen walked by. "Hen!" said Lily. A fuzzy bug crept up a leaf. "That one is a creeping thing," said Grandpa. "What will you call it?" Lily thought hard. "Mister Wiggles," she said. Grandpa laughed a big laugh. Then Lily tried to write the names. She did not know all the letters yet. But she knew A. A looks like a little tent. So she drew a tent for Adam at the top of the page. Grandpa showed her C. It is a circle with a bite out of it. C for the calf next door. Lily made a C, and a C, and a C, until she made a good one. At lunch Grandma set out warm bread. "B!" said Lily. "B is for bread. It has two bumps." She said thank You for the bread. Then she showed Grandma her page. A tent. Two bumps. A circle with a bite. "You are writing," said Grandma. Lily held her notebook close. Every name had letters. And now she could make them.

lil1-a-is-for-adam-who-named-the-animals.title: Bread for Today
lil1-a-is-for-adam-who-named-the-animals.body: One week, Sam's family did not have much food. Dad had been sick and could not work. The cupboard was almost empty. There was one loaf of bread left. At supper, Mom cut the bread into four pieces. One for Dad. One for Mom. One for Sam. One for baby June. Before they ate, they held hands. "Yahweh, thank You for our bread today," Dad prayed. "Please give us bread tomorrow too." Sam was quiet. He was a little worried. What about tomorrow? The next morning, someone knocked on the door. It was Mrs. Ortiz from church. She had a big bag in her arms. Inside were two loaves of bread, some eggs, and apples. "I baked too much," she said with a smile. Sam looked at the bag. On the side was a big letter B. B for bread. He traced it with his finger. Two bumps. That night, Sam prayed his own prayer. It was short. "Thank You for today's bread." Then he said one more thing. "And help me share some too." Mom hugged him. They had enough for today. And Yahweh had not forgotten them.

lil2-count-the-days-one-to-seven.title: Seven Stickers
lil2-count-the-days-one-to-seven.body: Ben had a paper chart on the fridge. It had seven boxes for seven days. Every night, Ben got to put one star sticker in a box. On day one, one star. "One!" said Ben. On day two, two stars. "Two!" Each night he counted them all again. On day four, Ben and Dad went outside after dark. They looked up. There was the moon. There were the stars. "Yahweh made these on day four," Dad said. "The sun for the day, and the moon for the night." On day five, Ben counted five stars. That was one whole hand! On day six, it was one hand and one more. Six. Ben was very tired by then. He had played hard all week. On day seven, he ran to the fridge for his last sticker. But Dad was sitting on the couch in his socks. Mom was reading a book. Nobody was in a hurry. "Today is our rest day," Mom said. "Yahweh worked six days, and then He rested." Ben put the seventh star in the last box. He counted them all. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. A whole week! Then he climbed up on the couch between Mom and Dad. And he rested too.

lil2-count-the-days-one-to-seven.title: Grandma Who Never Sat Down
lil2-count-the-days-one-to-seven.body: Grandma Rose worked every day. She swept the porch. She fed the hens. She washed and folded and baked. She worked on day one and day two. She worked on day five and day six. She even worked on day seven. One summer, Ruth came to stay. Ruth was six. She could count to seven. One night, Ruth saw Grandma rub her sore back. Grandma's eyes looked so tired. "Grandma," Ruth said, "how many days do you work?" Grandma counted on her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. All of them." Ruth shook her head. "Yahweh made the world in six days," she said. "On day seven, He rested. My teacher told me." Grandma was quiet for a long time. She looked at her seven fingers. Then she folded her hands in her lap. The next Sunday, the broom stayed in the corner. The hens got their food, but nobody baked. Grandma sat in her rocking chair. Ruth sat on the rug by her feet. They sang. They read. They took a nap in the sun. When Monday came, Grandma got up smiling. "I feel new," she said. Seven days make one week. And one of them is for rest.

lil3-big-and-small-goliath-and-the-musta.title: Measuring With My Arm
lil3-big-and-small-goliath-and-the-musta.body: Theo learned a new word at Sunday school. Cubit. A cubit is from your elbow to the tip of your finger. Theo came home and measured everything. He laid his arm on the couch. Elbow, finger. Elbow, finger. "The couch is five cubits!" he called. Then Dad measured the couch. Dad's arm was much longer. Elbow, finger. Elbow, finger. "Three cubits," said Dad. Theo frowned. "That is not fair. It is the same couch." Dad laughed. "My cubit is big. Your cubit is small. So we got different numbers." Then Theo had an idea. He stood by the kitchen door. "How tall was Goliath?" he asked. "Six cubits and a span," said Dad. So Dad measured up the wall with his long arm. One, two, three, four, five, six. Then he spread his hand wide for the span. His hand was way above the top of the door. Theo's mouth fell open. "He was taller than our door!" "Much taller," said Dad. Theo looked up and up. Then he looked at his own short arm. "I am small," he said. "But I can still measure big things." "You sure can," said Dad. And they measured the whole house before supper.

lil3-big-and-small-goliath-and-the-musta.title: The Seed in Ava's Hand
lil3-big-and-small-goliath-and-the-musta.body: Ava was the smallest one in her class. She could not reach the top shelf. She could not see over the big kids at the fair. Sometimes she felt like she did not matter much. One spring day, Grandpa put something in her hand. It was a tiny seed. It was smaller than a pea. "What can this do?" Ava asked. "It is so little." "Plant it and see," said Grandpa. So Ava dug a little hole by the fence. She dropped the seed in. She patted the dirt. She gave it water every day. For a long time, nothing happened. Ava wanted to give up. But Grandpa said, "Small things grow slowly. Keep watering." Then one morning, she saw a tiny green leaf. Then two leaves. Then a stem. By the end of summer, the plant was taller than Ava. One day a little bird flew down and sat in its branches. Ava stood very still and watched. "It was the smallest seed," she whispered. "And now a bird sits in it." Grandpa put his hand on her head. "Yahweh made that little seed," he said. "And He made you. Small is not the same as not important." Ava smiled. She was small. And she was growing.

lil4-sort-by-kind-two-by-two.title: Two by Two to the Toy Box
lil4-sort-by-kind-two-by-two.body: Eli had a toy ark and lots of toy animals. At clean-up time, they were everywhere. A giraffe was under the bed. Two pigs were in his sock drawer. A lion was in the bathtub. "Let's play Noah," Mom said. "The animals go in by kind." First Eli found all the birds. A blue bird. A red bird. A duck. "Birds go with birds," he said, and he lined them up. Then the cows. Then the bears. Then the fish, which did not need a boat at all. Eli laughed. "Fish can swim!" Next they marched the animals to the ark, two by two. "Two lions," said Mom. "Two, four, six," counted Eli as more went in. "Two sheep. Eight. Two camels. Ten." But then he found one zebra all by itself. "Where is the other zebra?" They looked and looked. Mom found it in the cat's bed. Eli laughed so hard he fell over. "Now there are two!" he said. In went the zebras. The ark was full. The floor was clean. Eli counted one last time, by twos, all the way to twenty. "Every kind is in," he said. And he set the ark on his shelf.

lil4-sort-by-kind-two-by-two.title: Two of Every Kind
lil4-sort-by-kind-two-by-two.body: One night a big storm came. Water got into a house on Maple Street. The family's beds got wet. Their coats got wet. Their shoes were ruined. Nobody was hurt, but they had to start again. The next day, Hannah's church put out big boxes. People brought clothes and shoes and blankets. Soon there was a huge pile. It was a mess. "We need sorters," said the pastor. "Who can sort by kind?" Hannah raised her hand. She was seven. She knew how to sort. She put coats with coats. Shoes with shoes. Blankets with blankets. Then she made sure every shoe had its partner. Two by two. Left and right. "One shoe all alone cannot help anybody," she said. She found lots of pairs. Two, four, six, eight, ten. When the family came, they did not have to dig through a mess. The boy found boots that fit right away. The mom found a warm coat. The little girl hugged a blue blanket and would not let go. Hannah watched from the corner. Her sorting had helped keep them warm. Sorting is not just a game. When things are put with their kind, people can find what they need.

lil5-first-words-from-the-word.title: Six Little Cards
lil5-first-words-from-the-word.body: Noah was four, and he wanted to read. His big sister Grace was teaching him. She wrote six words on six cards. Light. Good. Day. Night. Made. Love. "These are from the Bible," Grace said. "They are your first words." Every morning, Noah opened the curtains. Sun came pouring in. Grace held up a card. "Light," Noah read. Then another. "Day!" At bedtime, the room was dark. Grace held up a card. "Night," Noah read. Then she turned on his little lamp. "Light again!" he said. At supper, Dad said the soup was good. Noah jumped up and found the card. "Good!" he shouted. Everybody laughed. One evening, Noah pointed at his drawing on the fridge. "I made that," he said. Grace held up the card. Made. "And who made you?" she asked. "Yahweh made me," said Noah. Then came the last card. Noah knew the letters. L, o, v, e. He read it slowly. "Love." He looked at Grace. He looked at Mom and Dad. Then he gave the card to Grace. "For you," he said. Grace kept that card in her pocket for a whole year.

lil5-first-words-from-the-word.title: The Card for Mr. Hale
lil5-first-words-from-the-word.body: Mr. Hale lived alone in the gray house next door. His wife had gone to be with Yahweh. He did not wave much anymore. He just sat on his porch and looked at the street. Maya was five. She was learning to read and write. She knew some words now. Day. Night. Good. Love. One day, she asked Mom, "Is Mr. Hale sad?" "I think he is lonely," said Mom. Maya thought about it. Then she got paper and crayons. She drew a sun. She drew a flower. Then she wrote a word. She wrote it all by herself. L. O. V. E. The V was a little crooked. The E had too many lines. But it was the first word she ever wrote alone. She walked next door with Mom. She held out the card. Mr. Hale took it. He looked at it for a long time. Then he read it out loud, softly. "Love." His eyes got wet. "Did you write this?" he asked. Maya nodded. "It is my first word," she said. "I wanted it to be for you." Mr. Hale put the card in his front window. It stayed there all winter. And every morning after that, he waved.

lil6-how-many-loaves-how-many-baskets.title: Counting the Picnic
lil6-how-many-loaves-how-many-baskets.body: The whole family came to the park for a picnic. There were cousins everywhere. Aunts and uncles too. Too many to count! Jonah opened his lunch box. He had five crackers and two cheese sticks. "How many is that?" asked Aunt Bea. Jonah counted. "Five and two. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. Seven!" Then he looked at all the cousins. "That is not very much," he said. Aunt Bea smiled. She opened her basket. Uncle Lou opened his cooler. Grandma brought a whole pan of corn bread. Everybody put their food on the big blanket. Jonah put his seven pieces right in the middle. Then Grandpa said thank You to Yahweh for the food. Everyone ate. Everyone got full. When they were done, Jonah helped pick up what was left. He filled one basket. Then another. Then another. "Three baskets!" he said. "That is more than my whole lunch box." Grandma laughed. "That is what happens when everyone shares," she said. Jonah counted the baskets again, just to be sure. One, two, three. More than enough.

lil6-how-many-loaves-how-many-baskets.title: Grandpa Counts the Hens
lil6-how-many-loaves-how-many-baskets.body: Every night, Grandpa counted the hens. Lucy went with him. She held the flashlight. They counted at the door of the coop. "One, two, three," Grandpa said, as each hen went in. Lucy counted too. All the way to ten. Grandpa had ten hens. But one night, they only got to nine. Lucy counted again. Nine. "Pepper is missing," said Grandpa. Pepper was the little black hen with one white feather. She was Lucy's favorite. It was getting dark. It was getting cold. "We still have nine," Lucy said in a small voice. "Nine is a lot." Grandpa shut the coop door to keep the nine safe. Then he took the flashlight. "Nine is a lot," he said. "But Pepper is one of ours." They walked along the fence. They looked under the porch. They looked by the woodpile. Lucy called and called. At last, they heard a tiny cluck. Pepper was stuck in the berry bushes. Grandpa reached in very gently and lifted her out. Lucy held her close. She was warm. When they put her in the coop, they counted one more time. Ten. All of them. "Every one counts," said Grandpa. And Lucy hugged him tight.

lil7-adam-and-eve-made-loved-and-the-fir.title: Made Like Mama
lil7-adam-and-eve-made-loved-and-the-fir.body: Zoe looked in the mirror. Then she looked at Mama. "We have the same nose," she said. "And the same curly hair." Mama laughed. "That is because you came from me." Zoe thought about it. She looked at the picture of Grandma on the wall. The same nose again! Then Zoe went to her room and made something. She made a little clay girl. She gave it curly hair. She gave it a round nose. She even gave it a big smile, just like hers. She brought it to Mama. "I made this one like me," she said. "That is how Yahweh made people," said Mama. "He made them like Himself. In His image." "Is that why I like to make things?" Zoe asked. "Because He makes things?" "I think so," said Mama. "And it is why you can love, and laugh, and tell the truth." Zoe set the clay girl on the windowsill. She was very proud of it. She did not want anyone to drop it or break it. "I will take care of it," she said. "It is mine. I made it." Mama hugged her tight. "That is just how Yahweh feels about you," she said.

lil7-adam-and-eve-made-loved-and-the-fir.title: The One Rule
lil7-adam-and-eve-made-loved-and-the-fir.body: Dad built a tree house in the back yard. It had a rope swing and a little window. Dad gave Caleb only one rule. "Do not climb onto the roof," he said. "It is not safe yet. I still need to fix it." Caleb loved the tree house. He played in it every day. But one afternoon, his friend Max came over. "I bet you can see the whole town from the roof," Max said. "Your dad will never know." Caleb looked up at the roof. He knew the rule. But he climbed up anyway. Crack! A board broke. Caleb slid down and landed in the soft grass. He was not hurt, but the roof had a big hole in it. Caleb ran inside and hid behind the couch. His face felt hot. When Dad came home, he saw the hole. Then he found Caleb. Caleb waited for Dad to be very angry. But Dad sat down on the floor beside him. "Are you hurt?" Dad asked first. Caleb shook his head and began to cry. Dad held him. "You broke the one rule," Dad said softly. "And I still love you. I will make this right. I promise." That Saturday, Dad fixed the roof. Caleb handed him every nail.

lil8-noah-grace-the-door-yahweh-shut-and.title: Who Shut the Door?
lil8-noah-grace-the-door-yahweh-shut-and.body: The wind began to blow hard. Big dark clouds came over the hill. "A storm is coming!" called Dad. "Everybody inside." Mia and her little brother Leo ran up the steps. The dog ran in too. Then Leo turned around. He put both hands on the front door. He pushed with all his might. The wind pushed back. The door wobbled. "I will hold it shut!" Leo yelled. "I will keep us safe!" Mia tried to help him. They pushed and pushed. Their arms got tired. Then Dad came up behind them. He reached over their heads. He shut the door with one hand. Click went the lock. Leo looked up at him. "You do not have to hold it," Dad said with a smile. "I shut it. Now go get warm." So they did. They made a blanket fort in the living room. They ate popcorn. They listened to the rain go tap, tap, tap on the roof. The wind blew all night. But the door stayed shut. Leo fell asleep in the fort with the dog. He did not have to hold anything at all. Dad had shut the door, and that was enough.

lil8-noah-grace-the-door-yahweh-shut-and.title: The Bow After the Storm
lil8-noah-grace-the-door-yahweh-shut-and.body: The storm was very loud. Thunder boomed. Rain came down so hard that Ruby could not see the barn. A big branch fell off the old oak tree. Ruby hid her face in Mama's coat. She was scared the rain would never stop. "Will it rain forever?" she whispered. Mama held her close. "No, baby," she said. "Wait and see." After a long time, the thunder got quiet. The rain got soft. Then it stopped. Mama opened the door. The yard was full of puddles. The branch lay in the grass. Then Ruby looked up. Across the sky was a big bow of colors. Red and orange and yellow and green and blue and purple. "A rainbow," Ruby said. "Do you know what it means?" Mama asked. Ruby shook her head. "It is Yahweh's sign," Mama said. "It means He made a promise. And He remembers it, every time." Ruby looked at the bow for a long time. She did not feel scared anymore. That night, she drew a rainbow and taped it by her bed. When the next storm came, she looked at her picture. "He remembers," she said. And she went to sleep.

lil9-abraham-the-promise-the-stars-and-t.title: Too Many Stars
lil9-abraham-the-promise-the-stars-and-t.body: In the winter, Grandpa made Josie a promise. "When the warm days come," he said, "we will build you a swing." Josie believed him. She did not see a swing. The yard was full of snow. But she told everyone. "Grandpa is building me a swing." Her cousin Sam rolled his eyes. "Where is it?" he said. "I do not see it." "It is coming," said Josie. "Grandpa said so." One clear night, Grandpa took Josie outside. The sky was full of stars. "Count them," Grandpa said. Josie started. "One, two, three, four, five." She got to twenty. Then she got mixed up. She started again. Then she laughed. "Grandpa, nobody can count them all!" "That is right," said Grandpa. "Yahweh told Abraham to look at the stars. That is how big his family would be. Abraham did not have one child yet. But he believed Yahweh." Josie nodded. "Like I believe you about the swing." Grandpa laughed. "Like that," he said. When spring came, the snow melted. Grandpa got out his rope and a board. And there, under the big tree, was Josie's swing. Just like he said.

lil9-abraham-the-promise-the-stars-and-t.title: Going Without Knowing
lil9-abraham-the-promise-the-stars-and-t.body: One day Dad came home with news. "We are moving," he said. "I have a new job in a new town." Owen did not want to move. He loved his room. He loved his friends. He loved the big hill behind the house. "Where is the new house?" he asked. "What does it look like?" "We do not have a house yet," said Dad. "We will find one when we get there." That did not make Owen feel better. How could they go to a place they had never seen? The day came. They packed the truck. Owen held his teddy bear tight. He waved to his friend Micah from the window. Tears ran down his face. Dad drove a long, long way. Owen fell asleep. When he woke up, they were in a new town. They stayed in a small room for a few nights. Then they found a little yellow house. It had a tree in the yard and a window just for Owen. On the first Sunday, they went to a new church. A boy sat down beside Owen. "Want to play after?" he asked. Owen smiled for the first time in days. That night, Dad tucked him in. "We did not know where we were going," Owen said. "But Yahweh knew," said Dad.

mat1-count-and-place-value-the-numbers-h.title: The Penny Jar
mat1-count-and-place-value-the-numbers-h.body: Every year, the Carter kids emptied the big penny jar onto the kitchen table. This year, Nate went first. He counted one penny at a time. He got to two hundred and twelve. Then the dog barked, and he forgot where he was. He started over. He got to ninety-one. His little sister Tess sneezed. He started over again. Tess watched with her chin in her hands. Then she had an idea. She made a little pile of ten pennies. Then another. When she had ten piles of ten, she pushed them together and wrapped a paper strip around them. "That is one hundred," she said. Nate stopped and watched. Soon there were ten paper hundreds, and Tess put them in a shoebox. "A thousand," she said. Nate began to help. Tens, then hundreds, then thousands. Nobody lost count now, not even when the dog barked. When they finished, they wrote the total down. One thousand, three hundred and six. A 1 in the thousands place. A 3 in the hundreds. A 0 in the tens. A 6 in the ones. Mom checked it. Right the first time. "That is how Moses sorted a whole nation," she said. "Thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens."

mat1-count-and-place-value-the-numbers-h.title: The Zero in the Wrong Place
mat1-count-and-place-value-the-numbers-h.body: Every November, the church gathered cans for families who needed food. This year, twelve-year-old Daniel was in charge of the count. He took it seriously. He counted every can and wrote the total on the board: 1,050. On Saturday, the food bank sent a truck big enough for about a thousand cans. But when the helpers began loading, the cans kept coming. Box after box. The truck filled up, and cans were still stacked along the wall. Daniel's face went hot. He checked his notebook. He had counted one thousand five hundred cans, and then written it wrong. He had put the 5 in the tens place instead of the hundreds place. One digit in the wrong spot, and four hundred and fifty cans had disappeared on paper. The truck had to leave. Some families would wait another week. Daniel wanted to hide. Instead, Mr. Reyes sat down with him, and they wrote it out together. Thousands, hundreds, tens, ones. One, five, zero, zero. "Every place matters," Mr. Reyes said, "because every can is somebody's supper." Daniel called the food bank himself and asked for a second truck. It came on Monday. And from then on, Daniel read every number back by place, out loud, before he wrote it down.

mat2-adding-and-taking-away-loaves-fishe.title: What We Kept
mat2-adding-and-taking-away-loaves-fishe.body: Lena and her brother Max had a bake sale table at the church fair. Lena brought five loaves of banana bread. Max brought two trays of cookies. "Five plus two," Lena said, writing it on their sign. "Seven things to sell." By noon, everything was gone. They counted the money. Twelve dollars. Then Max frowned. "Wait. We spent money on flour and sugar and chocolate chips." He found the receipt. Seven dollars. "So we did not make twelve," said Lena. "We made twelve take away seven." Max counted back on his fingers. "Eleven, ten, nine, eight, seven. Five steps. We made five dollars." Lena was a little let down. Twelve sounded better. But Mrs. Patel at the next table leaned over. "Most people at this fair only tell you what they took in," she said. "You two figured out what you kept. That is real business." Max grinned. Lena wrote it neatly on the back of their sign for next year. Sold, twelve. Cost, seven. Kept, five. Next year they would buy flour in a big bag and save two dollars. That would make seven kept. They had already added it up.

mat2-adding-and-taking-away-loaves-fishe.title: The Ones Nobody Counted
mat2-adding-and-taking-away-loaves-fishe.body: Every summer, the youth group took three buses to help fix up homes in the next county. This year Ellie, who was eleven, got the job of planning lunches. Last year a grown-up had done it. He counted the kids on the list, added a few, and ordered sandwiches. But he never counted the bus drivers, or the families they were helping. On the last day, three drivers sat in the shade with nothing to eat, and a little boy from the house they were fixing watched the kids eat with big eyes. Ellie remembered that. So she counted carefully. Fifty-four kids. Plus nine adults. Fifty-four plus nine is sixty-three. Then she wrote a note at the bottom. Not counted yet: drivers, and the family at each house. Ask on the first day. On Monday, she asked. Three drivers. Two families, with eleven people between them. Sixty-three plus three plus eleven. Seventy-seven. She ordered eighty, just in case. At the end of the week, three lunches were left over, and Ellie handed them to the drivers for the ride home. Nobody had been left out. An honest count says what it knows. And it says out loud what it has not counted yet.

mat3-multiplying-and-sharing-thirtyfold-.title: Ninety Beans
mat3-multiplying-and-sharing-thirtyfold-.body: In April, Grandma gave Jack three bean seeds. "Plant them in the good soil by the fence," she said. "And pay attention." Jack wanted to see what would happen somewhere else too. So he planted one extra seed in the hard dirt by the driveway, where the gravel was. He watered them all. The seed by the driveway came up thin and yellow, and the hot sun burned it in a week. But the three by the fence grew and grew. They climbed the fence. They had flowers, and then pods, and then fat beans inside the pods. In August, Jack and Grandma picked them. Jack counted the beans from the first plant. Thirty. The second plant. Thirty again. The third. Thirty. "Three plants times thirty beans," said Grandma. "What does that make?" Jack added. "Thirty, sixty, ninety. Ninety beans!" "From three seeds," said Grandma. Jack looked over at the driveway. "And zero from that one," he said. "Zero times anything is still zero." Grandma laughed. "The same seed," she said. "Different ground." Jack saved twenty beans for next year. He knew exactly where he would plant them. If each one made thirty, that would be six hundred beans. He had already worked it out.

mat3-multiplying-and-sharing-thirtyfold-.title: The Tally on the Door
mat3-multiplying-and-sharing-thirtyfold-.body: Owen kept a tally on the inside of his closet door. Every time his little sister Pip broke one of his things, he made a mark. When she took his markers and left the caps off, a mark. When she knocked over his tower, a mark. When she spilled juice on his comic book, a mark. One day he showed Dad. "I forgave her forty-nine times," he said. "That is seven times seven. I counted." Dad looked at the marks for a long time. "That is good counting," he said. "Now let me show you a bigger one. Jesus said seventy times seven. Can you work it?" Owen thought. "Seven times seven is forty-nine. So seventy times seven is ten times that." He moved the digits over. "Four hundred ninety." "Right," said Dad. "Do you think Jesus wanted us to stop at four hundred ninety and start keeping score?" Owen did not answer. He looked at his marks. The numbers were real, and his math was right. But the tally felt heavy now, like a rock he had been carrying around in his closet. That night, he took an eraser to the door. It took a long time. Then he knocked on Pip's door. "Want to build a tower?" he asked.

mat4-parts-and-fractions-the-tenth-the-f.title: Ruth's First Forty Dollars
mat4-parts-and-fractions-the-tenth-the-f.body: Ruth was eleven, and she had just earned her first real money. She had walked Mrs. Kim's dog every afternoon for two weeks. Forty dollars, in four ten-dollar bills. She spread them on the bed and grinned. Dad sat down beside her with a pencil. "What will you do with it?" he asked. "Spend it," said Ruth. "All of it." "You could," Dad said. "But try it in parts first." He drew a long box and cut it into ten equal pieces. "The first tenth goes back to Yahweh. One tenth of forty." Ruth thought. "Forty shared into ten is four. So four dollars." She set them aside. "Now try saving a fifth," Dad said. He drew five pieces. Forty shared into five is eight. Ruth put eight dollars in her jar. "That leaves twenty-eight," she said. "Half of that could be for fun." Twenty-eight shared into two is fourteen. "So fourteen to spend," said Ruth, "and fourteen toward the bike." She laid it all out in neat piles. It did not look like less money anymore. It looked like a plan. On Sunday, she put her four dollars in the plate herself. And the bike jar grew a little every week.

mat4-parts-and-fractions-the-tenth-the-f.title: Ten Dollars and a Fifth
mat4-parts-and-fractions-the-tenth-the-f.body: Marcus found a wallet in the parking lot of the hardware store. Inside was a name, a phone number, and two twenty-dollar bills. He meant to call. He really did. But on the way home he stopped at the snack shop, and before he quite knew it, ten dollars was gone. That night, the wallet sat on his desk like it was staring at him. He told his mother everything. She did not yell. She was quiet, which was worse. "What do you think is right?" she asked. "Give back the ten," said Marcus. "Is that all?" Marcus remembered the Sunday lesson. When you take what is not yours, you give it back, and you add a fifth part more. "A fifth of ten," he said slowly. "Ten shared into five is two. So twelve dollars." He did yard work for two Saturdays to earn the twelve. Then he called the number. An old man answered. Marcus rode his bike across town and handed him the wallet, with forty dollars inside and two more on top. He told the truth about all of it. The old man was quiet for a while. Then he shook Marcus's hand. "The money is not the part I will remember," he said.

mat5-measure-cubits-spans-ephahs-and-jus.title: Whose Cubit?
mat5-measure-cubits-spans-ephahs-and-jus.body: Abby and her dad were building a wooden toy chest for her baby cousin. Abby had a plan. She had read about the ark of the covenant, a box two cubits and a half long and a cubit and a half wide. "Let's make it that size," she said. So she measured the long boards with her arm. Elbow to fingertip, two and a half times. Dad cut where she marked. Then Dad measured the end pieces with his own arm. A cubit and a half. He cut those too. When they tried to nail it together, nothing fit. The end pieces were almost as long as the sides. The box came out nearly square, and the lid would not close. Abby stared at it. Then she laughed. "Your cubit is bigger than mine!" Dad held his arm next to hers. Her cubit was about twelve inches. His was about eighteen. "That is why builders agree on one measure," Dad said. "One cubit for the whole job, the same every time." So they marked one true cubit on a stick, eighteen inches long, and used only that. They measured twice and cut once. The new box was square, and the lid shut with a soft thump. Abby kept the stick and wrote CUBIT on it in big letters.

mat5-measure-cubits-spans-ephahs-and-jus.title: The Bent Spring
mat5-measure-cubits-spans-ephahs-and-jus.body: Mr. Odom sold tomatoes and peaches at a farm stand on the county road. His granddaughter Lucy, who was ten, helped him on Saturdays. She loved to work the old hanging scale. She put the fruit in the pan and read the needle. One pound. Two pounds. One Saturday, a man with a stand of his own down the road stopped by. He laughed when he saw the scale. "Want to make more money?" he said. "Bend the spring a little. Every pound reads a pound and a quarter. Nobody ever checks." Lucy looked at her grandpa.
